World.title: Polish court finds regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage registration unconstitutional
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. Nielegalny Trybunał Konstytucyjny po raz kolejny próbuje zatrzymać państwo, które wykonuje obowiązujące prawo i wyroki europejskich sądów. Transkrypcja zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych jest i będzie legalna. Rozporządzenie, które przyjęliśmy porządkuje dokumenty i… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. World.title: Residents oppose move to add Polish village to list of protected monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. World.title: Poland enters race to host EU-backed AI gigafactory
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. It will help write letters, analyse inquiries from residents, and summarise long documents https://t.co/SLrmVg9VBz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 Earlier this month, Poland’s government approved a resolution enabling the country to participate in the European AI Gigafactory programme, committing more than 400 million zloty towards what the government says would be the largest computing centre in the country’s history. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. Bidding consortia will have 15 weeks to submit proposals, contracts are due to be awarded in early 2027 and the facilities are scheduled to become operational in 2028. 🚀 Droga do Gigafabryki AI otwarta. World.title: Prague Pride Strengthens Security Measures Following Berlin Attack
World.content:
Security will be tightened at this year’s Prague Pride festival following a deadly attack at a similar event in Berlin.

Czech police are preparing additional measures to protect participants in the week-long festival, which begins Monday.

The measures will also reflect changes to this year’s festival route and venue.

Prague Pride is moving its main festival area from Letná Plain to Štvanice Island. The traditional Saturday parade will also follow a new route, starting in the lower section of Wenceslas Square, continuing through the historic center and ending at Štvanice.



Organizers will begin the parade with a minute of silence on Wenceslas Square to remember the person killed in the Berlin attack.

“Thousands of people standing in silence will be a reminder that we will definitely not remain silent about violence motivated by prejudice,” Prague Pride director Kamila Fröhlichová said.

This year’s Prague Pride will feature more than 100 cultural, educational and social events. Dozens of associations, institutions, companies and individuals will organize programs at venues across the capital.

While many events will focus on the lives and experiences of LGBTQ+ people, the festival will also address wider questions surrounding human rights and civil society. A full program is available on the Prague Pride website.

Prague Pride was first held in August 2011. Its inaugural edition was met with strong opposition from conservative groups and politicians, who described the parade as obscene and accused its organizers of promoting what they called an “ideology of homosexuality.”

Then-President Václav Klaus was among the most prominent critics, arguing that society needed to oppose what he described as the spread of homosexuality.

Protests continued in subsequent years but gradually declined in size and intensity.

World.title: Prague Opens Air-Conditioned Space in City Centre to Help Beat Heat Wave
World.content:
People looking for relief from the heat in central Prague can use the air-conditioned ground floor of the Škoda Palace in Jungmannova Street on Thursday and Friday.

The city has opened the space to the public as temperatures across the Czech Republic are expected to rise well above 30°C. The building will be accessible from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on both days.

Visitors can sit on benches and chairs, refill their water bottles at drinking fountains and use the toilets. Drinks and snacks are also available for purchase.



The measure comes as the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute has warned of very high temperatures in parts of the country. Forecasters are advising people to drink regularly, stay out of direct sunlight where possible and avoid strenuous physical activity, particularly during the afternoon.

The Czech Republic is facing several days of intense heat, with Friday expected to be among the hottest day of the current spell. Temperatures above 35°C are possible in some areas.

Individual Prague districts are taking similar steps. Prague 3, for example, plans to make air-conditioned areas in its town hall, information centre and Žižkostel available to the public when temperatures are forecast to exceed 35°C. Visitors will be able to sit down, drink water and take a break from the heat.

The city says the cooling spaces are intended to provide temporary relief during the hottest periods, particularly for people who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.

World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Babiš Warns Czechia Could Become Net EU Payer by 2029 as Contributions Surge
World.content:
The Czech prime minister also said Brussels is likely to permit a larger budget deficit as Prague seeks funding for hospitals, highways, and other domestic investment.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has expressed alarm over the country’s rapidly increasing payments to the European Union, warning that the Czech Republic could become a net contributor to the bloc as early as 2029.

Following talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, Babiš said Czech payments into the EU budget had risen by 22 billion crowns (€911 million) this year alone.

“I was shocked by how much we are paying into the European Union,” he said, as cited by Echo24. “If in one year we are told that we will pay 22 billion more, that is a lot.”



Officials currently expect the Czech Republic to become a net contributor to the EU budget for the first time in its history in either 2029 or 2030.

Babiš was also asked about next year’s state budget deficit. When asked whether it would exceed this year’s planned shortfall of 310 billion crowns (€12.8 billion), he replied, “Don’t test me. I don’t know what the deficit will be.”

Schillerová said a reliable estimate would only be possible after the Finance Ministry publishes its updated economic forecast next month.

The government has informed the European Commission that it expects next year’s structural deficit to reach as much as 2.9 percent of GDP, compared with 2.4 percent this year. According to Schillerová, Brussels has provisionally accepted the higher ceiling.

“We have to invest in hospitals, highways and bypasses,” he said, justifying the overspend but maintaining that the deficit should remain significantly below 400 billion crowns (€16.6 billion).

Planned spending includes psychiatric hospitals, surgical facilities, oncology centers, highways and city bypasses. The government also intends to maintain defense expenditure at 2 percent of GDP.

World.title: Hundreds of Czech Castles and Chateaus to Offer Free Entry on Two Special Days
World.content:
Visitors will be able to explore more than 100 state-managed castles, chateaus, monasteries, and other historic landmarks across Czechia free of charge on August 30 and September 27.

The initiative follows a spring pilot program that granted free admission to selected state museums and galleries. According to the Ministry, strong public interest in that campaign encouraged officials to extend the concept to historic monuments managed by the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ).

The free admission will apply to the standard sightseeing route at each participating site, along with selected additional visitor circuits where available.



Tours will operate under normal conditions, meaning visitor numbers will remain limited and capacity restrictions will continue to apply.

The National Heritage Institute is expected to publish a complete list of participating sites, opening hours, reservation requirements, and visitor information on its website in the coming days.

The latest initiative builds on an earlier trial introduced this spring.

Between April and June, visitors were granted free entry on selected Sundays to five of the country’s largest state museums: the National Museum in Prague, the Moravian Museum in Brno, the Silesian Museum in Opava, the National Technical Museum in Prague, and the Technical Museum in Brno.

According to the Ministry of Culture, attendance at those museums nearly doubled during the pilot period, with the Silesian Museum recording the largest increase in visitor numbers. Selected state galleries also participated in the program earlier this year while officials assessed the financial impact of waiving admission fees.

The ministry has said one of its long-term objectives is to help restore visitor numbers at cultural institutions to levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: On this Day, in 1419: the First Defenestration of Prague
World.content:
Six hundred years ago, an angry crowd stormed Prague’s New Town Hall and threw several royal councillors from its windows.

The attack, known as the First Defenestration of Prague, took place on July 30, 1419, and is widely regarded as the event that ignited the Hussite Wars—a conflict that transformed medieval Bohemia and left a lasting mark on Czech history.

Yet the violence that unfolded that summer day had been years in the making.

Its roots lay in the teachings of Jan Hus, a Czech theologian, university lecturer, and religious reformer who became one of the most influential figures of the late Middle Ages. Hus openly criticized corruption within the Catholic Church, particularly the sale of indulgences and the growing power of the church hierarchy. Rather than viewing the Church as an institution led by the pope and bishops, he argued that the true Church was the community of faithful believers.

Summoned before the Council of Constance in 1415 to defend his beliefs, Hus was arrested despite receiving a promise of safe conduct. After refusing to renounce his teachings, he was convicted of heresy and burned at the stake.



His execution outraged many across Bohemia. While members of the nobility saw it as the unjust killing of one of the kingdom’s own, Hus’s followers spread his ideas far beyond Prague through a network of priests and former university students. The capital, home to Charles University and the Bethlehem Chapel where Hus had preached, became the center of a rapidly growing reform movement.

Bohemia’s political circumstances also allowed the movement to flourish. Neither King Wenceslas IV nor the Archbishop of Prague took decisive action to suppress it, allowing religious tensions to deepen over the following years.

By the summer of 1419, the situation had reached a breaking point.

On July 30, radical Hussite preacher Jan Želivský led a religious procession through Prague after delivering an impassioned sermon. Although the march may have appeared spontaneous, historians believe the confrontation had been carefully prepared. Some participants reportedly arrived carrying concealed weapons, expecting violence.

The procession made its way to Prague’s New Town Hall, demanding the release of Hussite supporters imprisoned there. When the councillors refused, the crowd forced its way inside.

The assault was led by Jan Žižka, a military commander who would later become one of medieval Europe’s greatest generals. Several councillors were seized and thrown from the building’s windows. Although the fall itself was not fatal for everyone, those who survived were beaten to death by the waiting crowd below.

For medieval society, the act carried a powerful symbolic meaning. Publicly casting powerful officials from an elevated position represented the dramatic downfall of those who had abused their authority.

The defenestration did not, by itself, begin the Hussite Wars, but it made peaceful reconciliation increasingly unlikely. Just weeks later, King Wenceslas IV died, leaving the throne to his brother Sigismund, whom many Bohemians blamed for failing to protect Jan Hus at Constance. Relations between the Hussites and the crown rapidly collapsed, and in 1420 the first crusade against Bohemia was launched.

The wars that followed lasted more than a decade. They devastated much of the kingdom but also produced extraordinary military victories under Jan Žižka and established the Hussites as one of medieval Europe’s most formidable fighting forces.

The First Defenestration of Prague remains one of the defining moments in Czech history—a single act of violence that turned years of religious unrest into a revolution whose legacy can still be seen throughout the country today.

World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Number of insolvencies in Romanian agriculture increases 80% YoY in H1 2026
World.content:
The number of agricultural companies entering insolvency procedures has reached an unprecedented level in recent years, according to an analysis carried out by insolvency and restructuring consultant CITR based on data provided by the National Trade Register Office.

Insolvencies in agriculture recorded an increase of almost 80%, from 127 cases in H1 2025 to 226 cases in H1 2026. Moreover, by mid-April 2026, the number of insolvencies in agriculture had already reached the level recorded during the entire first half of last year.

Insolvencies exploded particularly among companies with fixed assets exceeding EUR 4 million, from a single company in H1 2025 to 19 companies in H1 2026. The latter concentrate more than EUR 235 million in fixed assets, equivalent to more than 57% of the total assets that entered insolvency in this segment across the entire economy.

According to CITR, the increase in the number of insolvencies in the agricultural sector over six months reflects an accumulation of structural and cyclical pressures on Romanian farmers. Profit margins have been compressed under the combined effect of volatile grain prices, high production and financing costs, and recurring droughts. As a result, an increasing share of farmers is reorienting toward autumn crops, which are more stable than corn or sunflower. Added to this are the pressure from grain imports from Ukraine and the rising cost of energy and fertilizers amid geopolitical instability.

“If in previous years the vulnerabilities in agriculture were absorbed mainly by small or family farms, in the first half of 2026 we are witnessing an expansion of the crisis toward impactful companies, with extensive networks of suppliers, distributors and financiers. When a large player in agriculture enters payment incapacity, the wave is immediately transmitted throughout the local and regional supply chain,” said Paul-Dieter Cîrlănaru, CEO of CITR.

The CITR analysis carried out on a representative sample of 3,700 agricultural companies, out of a total of 13,700 that filed financial statements and have total assets of at least EUR 1 million, indicated a worrying structural vulnerability. Roughly 40% of the companies are already in the high financial risk zone. 631 companies are in imminent insolvency, and 855 companies are classified as restructurable, urgently needing operational and financial reorganization measures.

Companies at risk that nevertheless have solid turnover and a significant number of employees represent priority cases for early restructuring intervention, which can prevent cascading social and economic effects.

The insolvency situation of the agricultural sector is also illustrated by the evolution of the non-performing loan rate among non-financial companies, which, according to the National Bank of Romania’s Financial Stability Report published in June 2026, rose to 5.6%, while in the micro and small enterprise segment it exceeds 7%.

Loans backed by state guarantees, used extensively in agriculture during 2020–2022, have a non-performing rate of 11.3%, a sign that the emergency support granted at that time did not generate the expected resilience.

Thus, the main centers of large insolvencies are the counties of Bacău and Hunedoara, followed by Vaslui, Bihor and Ialomița, areas dependent on extensive agriculture where large companies with assets exceeding EUR 4 million are in insolvency. Timiș, Bucharest, Arad, Constanța, and Teleorman followed in the ranking of counties by the total number of agricultural companies at risk.

World.title: French court definitively rejects appeal filed by Paul of Romania against extradition
World.content:
France’s Court of Cassation has definitively rejected the appeal filed by Paul of Romania against his extradition to Romania for the execution of his jail sentence.

The ruling, given on Wednesday, July 29, makes final the “decision to execute the European arrest warrant and to surrender the requested person to Romania,” according to the Romanian Ministry of Justice, cited by News.ro.

“The decision of the French supreme court reconfirms the effective judicial cooperation between Romania and the French Republic and the common commitment of the two states to applying the principles of the rule of law and respecting the obligations assumed within the European mechanisms of judicial cooperation. At the same time, this ruling confirms the proper functioning of the European arrest warrant, an important instrument of judicial cooperation in criminal matters at the level of the European Union,” the statement of the Ministry of Justice added.

Former justice minister Radu Marinescu weighed in on the ruling, arguing that it is a remarkable success for the Romanian judicial authorities.

“After several successive refusals of surrender, we persevered, the CJEU was notified and ruled in Romania’s favor, we returned with the surrender request, and in the end we triumphed definitively,” the former minister said.

He added that Paul of Romania joins the list of well-known convicted or criminally investigated persons brought to Romania.

On June 19, the Ministry of Justice announced that the judicial authorities in Paris had ordered the immediate surrender of Paul of Romania to the Romanian authorities, but the decision was not final.

Paul, the descendant of King Carol II, one of Romania’s last kings, is accused of having collaborated with a gang of fraudsters, beginning in 2006, in order to recover properties he claimed as an heir to the royal family. He was sentenced to three years and four months in prison for influence peddling and complicity in 2020, along with 17 others. The damage caused to the Romanian state was estimated to be at least EUR 145 million.

The Paris Court of Appeal rejected the first extradition request in November 2023, considering that the right to a fair trial had not been respected, given the irregularities found in the oath-taking of two of the three judges who convicted him.

Romanian authorities issued a new arrest warrant against the prince in January 2025, based on the ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) of July 29, 2024, delivered following a preliminary reference request. The CJEU considered that the decision of the French judiciary was “contrary to the principle of mutual trust” between European countries, exercising “excessive control” over the functioning of the Romanian judicial system.

Paul of Romania was arrested at his residence in Paris and imprisoned on April 7, 2025, and was subsequently placed under judicial supervision. Paul’s lawyer denounced “the greatest political scandal ever experienced by a royal family,” in connection with the “inheritance dispute.”

World.title: First contingent of 40 Romanian firefighters stationed in Greece to help battle forest fires
World.content:
A first contingent of 40 Romanian firefighters will be in Greece starting on August 1, 2026, to support local teams battling fires that have broken out amid high summer temperatures.

The firefighters left on Thursday, July 30, for a locality in the Attica region, located approximately 25 kilometres northeast of Athens. The move is part of the pre-positioning programme organized by the Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG ECHO).

“For the fulfilment of the mission, the national module has two forest fire extinguishing vehicles with a capacity of 3,000 litres, one 5,000-litre vehicle, one high-capacity 10,000-litre vehicle, one 30,000-litre tanker, one first intervention and command vehicle equipped with an unmanned aircraft system, one shortwave radio communications vehicle, one minibus, one container truck and one utility terrain vehicle equipped with fire extinguishing installations,” Romania’s General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations said in a statement posted to Facebook.

To ensure the continuity of the mission, the rotation of personnel is scheduled for August 16 and 31, 2026, when two other contingents, each consisting of 40 firefighters, will take over the duties of the personnel deployed near Athens.

According to the same source, the pre-positioning programme has as its main objectives reducing response time in the event of forest fires, increasing the level of preparedness of the intervention modules of the member states and strengthening interoperability among the participating forces. Throughout the mission, the Romanian module specialized in forest fire extinguishing will carry out monitoring and intervention activities to contain and extinguish fires that break out on the territory of Greece, in the areas established by the Greek authorities.

The assistance programme, financed by the European Union, was designed as a support measure for communities in Europe severely affected by the devastating fires of previous years. It is part of the EU’s new policy for preventing and limiting forest fires in southern Europe and brings together this year, on the territory of the Hellenic Republic, operational crews from Romania, the Czech Republic, France and Moldova.

World.title: Colliers: Romania land market slows in H1, developers position for 2027-2028
World.content:
Romania's land market remained active in the first half of 2026 despite a slowdown in completed transactions, as developers continued acquiring sites for projects expected to reach the market in 2027-2028, according to a new report by real estate consultancy Colliers. Retail remained the strongest-performing segment, while residential land continued to attract investor interest despite a period of market adjustment.

Colliers said numerous land transactions are currently under negotiation or at the pre-contract stage, but relatively few large deals were finalized in the first six months of the year amid uncertainty over energy costs, construction budgets, and the domestic political environment.

“The land market is going through a period of repositioning; it is by no means at a standstill. We are seeing a significant number of discussions, negotiations, and transactions in progress, even though fewer large deals were completed in the first half of the year," said Sînziana Oprea, director of Land Agency at Colliers Romania.

She added that retail remains the most active segment, while residential land continues to attract interest, including from new market entrants, although buyers are negotiating more cautiously and putting greater pressure on pricing, payment terms, and permitting certainty.

According to the report, demand for retail land remains robust across Romania, supported by the continued expansion of discount, food, and DIY retailers, particularly in smaller cities. Residential land also continues to attract interest, including from international investors, with some major developers increasingly looking beyond Bucharest to regional cities.

The industrial land segment, however, remains subdued, as many investors already have sufficient land reserves and are waiting for better opportunities before making new acquisitions. Colliers noted growing interest instead in specialist projects such as student housing, medical facilities, and educational developments.

The consultancy also said infrastructure continues to shape investment decisions, with the Bucharest A0 ring road generating stronger investor interest than planned subway extensions.

At the same time, the number of land plots offered for sale has increased, partly because institutional and international investors are considering exits amid political uncertainty.

“Supply is more substantial than in the past, and this is changing the balance of negotiations. […] Buyers are responding very cautiously: they are more selective, negotiate more carefully, and are in a stronger position than during the years when the market was dominated by sellers," Oprea said.

Colliers expects selective price increases of 5-10% for prime plots with strong development potential and advanced permitting, while sites with weaker planning documentation or limited access could come under downward price pressure.

Looking ahead, the consultancy said the current pace of acquisitions suggests developers are preparing for the next real estate cycle rather than responding to immediate market conditions.

“For developers, land acquired today is not a bet on the current market, but a way of positioning themselves for the market of 2027-2028. […] Those making decisions during this period are already looking towards the next growth cycle,” Sînziana Oprea said.

World.title: Developer Urban Spaces seeks EUR 1.3 mln for Bucharest build-to-rent project via Growceanu
World.content:
Romanian residential developer Urban Spaces announced the launch of its first public fundraising campaign, seeking EUR 1.3 million for the build-to-rent component of its Urban Spaces Aviației project in Bucharest. The campaign is being conducted through Growceanu, a regulated Romanian investment platform for private companies.

The funding round, open until September 30, represents 20% of the capital of the Urban Spaces BTR company and is open to both individual and corporate investors.

Urban Spaces BTR is part of the mixed-use Urban Spaces Aviației development, the company's largest project to date, with an estimated value of EUR 150 million. The overall project will comprise more than 400 apartments, alongside office, retail, and leisure spaces.

The build-to-rent component includes 32 apartments and 13 underground parking spaces, which are planned to be professionally managed and rented on short-, medium- and long-term leases. Thanks to flexible layouts, the apartments can be configured as up to 40 accommodation units, the company said.

Around 70% of the invested capital is expected to be returned after the development phase, with the remaining investment generating income through the operation of the rental units.

“For the first time, we are opening up the opportunity for investors to join us in developing an Urban Spaces project through a regulated investment platform," said Gavril Zaharia, CEO and co-founder of Urban Spaces.

The campaign also marks Growceanu's first real estate offering, expanding the platform beyond its traditional focus on technology companies.

World.title: Romanian major bank BRD posts 2.5% increase in net profit in H1 2026
World.content:
BRD (BVB: BRD), one of the major banks present in Romania, reported a net profit of RON 784 million in the first half of the year, up 2.5%, according to the report submitted to the Bucharest Stock Exchange.

In H1 2026, BRD Group’s net banking income reached RON 2,206 million, up +1.8% year-on-year. Net interest income, which accounts for 70% of net banking income, totaled RON 1,548 million in H1 2026, up +1.4% year-on-year.

Net fee and commission income amounted to RON 452 million, compared with RON 453 million in H1 2025, remaining broadly stable compared with the previous year. Increased customer activity and the solid contribution of custody, brokerage, asset management and off-balance-sheet commitment activities were offset by the decrease in fee income from services, amid the process of cleaning inactive accounts.

Other banking income reached RON 206 million, up +9% year-on-year, mainly reflecting higher income related to associated entities, as well as the recognition of an exceptional (“one-off”) income.

In the context of persistent double-digit inflation and the doubling of the turnover tax, operating expenses decreased by 0.5% year-on-year in H1 2026, supported by cost discipline and the absence of contributions to the Deposit Guarantee Fund and the Resolution Fund (FGDB and FR) in 2026. Personnel expenses decreased by 8.3% year-on-year, reflecting the optimization of the Group’s workforce activity and operating model.

Excluding the turnover tax and the cumulative contributions to guarantee funds related to 2025, the other categories of operating expenses increased by +3.1% year-on-year, mainly as a result of higher IT&C expenses, generated by the depreciation of previous investments and the continuation of infrastructure and digitalization projects.

The turnover tax for the January-June 2026 period doubled compared with H1 2025, reaching RON 139 million (equivalent to 4% of gross revenues), compared with RON 66 million in the same period of the previous year.

In this context, BRD Group’s gross operating profit increased by +4.2% year-on-year, to RON 1,112 million in H1 2026.

The cost/income ratio improved to 49.6%, compared with 50.7% in H1 2025. Excluding the impact of the turnover tax and other contributions related to 2025, the cost/income ratio would have stood at 43.3% in H1 2026, compared with 45.4% in H1 2025, representing an improvement of 214 basis points.

BRD's non-performing loan ratio at the bank level reached 2.7% at the end of June 2026, below the banking system average of 2.9% recorded at the end of May 2026, while the coverage ratio for non-performing loans remained at a comfortable level of 65.6%. Net cost of risk recorded a limited increase compared with the same period of the previous year, with a net allocation of provisions of RON 147 million, compared with RON 142 million in H1 2025, amid the combined effect of portfolio developments and the revision of macroeconomic outlooks.

BRD Group recorded a net profit of RON 784 million in H1 2026, up 2.5% compared with the level of RON 764 million recorded in H1 2025. Excluding the impact of the turnover tax, return on equity (ROE) stood at 17%, compared with 17.3% one year earlier.

BRD’s capital adequacy ratio, at the individual level, stood at 22% at the end of June 2026, stable compared with the end of June 2025 (excluding the impact of temporary regulatory treatments, “quick fix”).

Net outstanding loans, including leasing financing, reached RON 58.3 billion, up +11.6% year-on-year (of which financial leasing receivables increased by +1.6% year-on-year). Growth was recorded both in the corporate segment and in retail, despite persistent macroeconomic difficulties. Corporate lending was the main driver of portfolio expansion (+16.5% year-on-year), supported by strong commercial activity in the large corporate segment. Retail loans also made a solid contribution, with net loan balances increasing by +8.0%, supported by resilient demand for housing loans.

In the first half of 2026, BRD continued to expand its sustainable financing activity, with cumulative production of EUR 2.63 billion since 2021, of which EUR 304 million was granted in H1 2026. At the same time, the bank assumed important roles in structuring sustainable financing, both independently and together with Societe Generale.

The total deposit base reached RON 73.7 billion, up +4.1% year-on-year, amid higher inflows from individual customers. Retail deposits, a stable and diversified source of financing, increased by +7.4% year-on-year, due to attracting a higher volume from individual customers. Corporate deposits recorded a decrease of -1.1% year-on-year, mainly reflecting balance sheet adjustments to liquidity conditions, market conditions, and the fluctuating financing needs of large companies.

World.title: Serbian Feminists Expect Boost From Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law
World.content:
Serbian women’s rights organisations say they feel encouraged by developments in neighbouring Montenegro, which has adopted law changes introducing two paid days of “menstrual leave” per month for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea, or severe menstrual cramp.

“It has generated considerable enthusiasm among women. It feels like a very progressive idea and a major step forward, especially if we take into account that no country in the wider region has a law introducing such measures,” said Ljiljana Todorovic Jovanovic, founder of the FemIn Collective, a women’s rights NGO from Pozarevac.

The news from Montenegro has been hailed by Serbian women’s rights groups but criticised by some of the general public, activists said.

“Part of the general public welcomed the move and expressed hope that something similar would be introduced in Serbia. However, another part interpreted the news as meaning that women had been granted some kind of privilege,” Ana Mirkailo, an activist from Befem, a Belgrade-based feminist cultural centre and NGO founded in 2009, told BIRN.

She added that this divided reaction didn’t surprise her but “served as a reminder of how much work still needs to be done in this area”.

Spain was the first country in Europe to introduce paid “menstrual leave” in 2023, followed by Portugal, which has allowed up to three consecutive paid days off per month since 2025 for people experiencing disabling pain caused by diagnosed endometriosis or adenomyosis.

The Montenegrin measure applies to women suffering from serious conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace, and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

Todorovic Jovanovic said women in Serbia with menstrual health problems can already take ordinary sick leave, during which they receive 65 per cent of their salary. The problem, however, is that employers do not always respond well when employees request sick leave.

“On paper, the law allows workers to take sick leave simply by visiting a doctor, but there are employers and workplaces where taking leave is effectively impossible – whether to care for a child, because of illness, or due to menstrual health problems,” Todorovic Jovanovic said, adding that even if a similar law as Montenegro’s were adopted, the question of implementation in practice would remain.

For years there have been attempts in Serbia to address menstrual health issues as part of women’s general health, and put them up for discussion.

Last year, a Menstrual Justice Initiative was established in Serbia, bringing together researchers and several women’s organisations from across the country. The initiative was created to advocate for greater recognition of menstrual health and related rights.

The latest law changes in Montenegro have given Menstrual Justice Initiative fresh momentum.

“Women’s organisations actively monitor and listen to the communities they work with, and it is important to respond to that momentum. Legislative initiatives of this kind should originate from women’s organisations and be developed in cooperation with political actors who demonstrate a genuine willingness to support them,” Mirkailo said.

Both Todorovic Jovanovic and Mirkailo agreed that menstrual leave is not a “privilege” and that the question of menstrual leave is not only a question of health but of obtaining work-based rights for those who need them.

Todorovic Jovanovic, from Femin Collective, which is a member of the Menstrual Justice Initiative, explains that two main advocacy models are being pursued in the region. The first focuses on reducing VAT on menstrual products, while the second concerns the introduction of “menstrual leave”, as in Montenegro.

North Macedonia currently has the lowest VAT rate on menstrual products in the region, at 5 per cent, compared with 20 per cent in Serbia and 21 per cent in Montenegro.

“What we have been considering is initially directing our advocacy efforts towards reducing VAT, based on research conducted by the Gender Knowledge Hub, which reported in 2023 that women needed about 8,300 dinars (70 euros) a year to cover the cost of menstrual products,” Todorovic Jovanovic said.

She explained that this becomes particularly significant when it is considered how many women come from socially disadvantaged groups and cannot afford these essential products.

World.title: Live From Manhattan: Bosnia’s Republika Srpska and a Selective View of the Past
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

In late July, Denis Bojic, the director of the Republika Srpska Memorial Centre, told the Serbian daily newspaper Politika: “The politics of memory is a means of survival.”

Bojic was commenting on the Centre’s recent campaign in New York, in which billboards bearing photographs and accounts testifying to the ‘suffering’ of the Serb people travelled through Manhattan.

Bojic’s words offered perhaps the clearest explanation of the campaign’s political significance. If Republika Srpska, the predominantly Serb-populated entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were denied the right to tell the world about Serb suffering, he said, it would mean “the end of the existence of Republika Srpska”.

‘Learn About Serbian Suffering’ was presented in New York on July 10 and 11 by the Memorial Centre, a public institution established by the Republika Srpska government in 2024.

According to the organisers, the exhibition appeared at a number of prominent locations in the city, including near the headquarters of the United Nations. A QR code was displayed, directing interested passers-by to a digital collection of testimonies and archival material.

Even the timing of the exhibition was political.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Two on War Crime Allegations Amid Mass Grave Excavation
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



The alleged mass grave location in Kalluder, near Zubin Potok. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court ordered 30 days’ detention to two Serbs suspected of war crimes during the 1999 war in Kosovo.

The suspects, M.J. and M.B., were arrested on Monday in a police operation. The prosecution says the case is related to the ongoing excavation of a suspected mass grave near Zubin Potok in northern Kosovo.

The works, which started on Monday, are being conducted on the request of the Special Prosecution and by order of the Court of Pristina for exhumation, autopsy and identification of mortal remains.

“The court assessed that the imposition of pre-trial detention in this criminal case is an adequate measure, as there is a real risk that if the defendants are released, they may flee with the aim of hiding and escaping criminal responsibility; also, taking into account that the defendants are also citizens of Serbia, there is a real risk that they will easily flee,” the court said on Wednesday.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Albin Kurti echoed suspicions that the grave might hold the remains of 23 Albanian civilians from Mitrovica who were taken by Serbian forces on April 19, 1999 and never found since.

“Our immediate suspicion when we learned that mortal remains were found was that it was the group of 23 intellectuals in Mitrovica who were kidnapped and forcibly disappeared. We cannot confirm that it is them, but this was our immediate suspicion. However, we must wait for our institutions to tell us what it is about,” Kurti said.

“But it seems that we have a mass grave in the village of Kalluder, Zubin Potok, in the north, which was an area that had not been examined before,” he added.

Kushtrim Gara, from the Kosovo government’s commission on missing persons, said the location has been in the focus of relevant institutions for a long time but did not give more details due to the sensitivity of the case.

“We are waiting for the completion of all examinations and the exhumation process, and any information that can be shared will initially be shared with the families of the missing persons, because the victims are at the centre of this process,” Gara said.

On July 28, the Serbian government’s Office for Kosovo criticised the arrests and accused the Kosovo authorities of putting local Serbs under undue pressure.

“These unfounded actions add to the unrest in Serbian communities and create a sense of insecurity and fear among the Serbian people, which is the goal of the regime in Pristina, which has no political legitimacy and is trying to build its position by oppressing the Serbian people,” the office said.

A report published on Wednesday by Kosovo’s Institute of Crimes Committed During the War concluded that 1,578 persons are still missing from the 1999 Kosovo war.

World.title: Former Turkish PM Davutoglu Quits Politics After Failing to Unite Conservatives
World.content:
Former Turkish Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu announced on Wednesday that he is leaving politics and is dissolving his failing Future Party.

“We have decided to withdraw from party politics and bring the Future Party’s political activities to an end, in order to avoid becoming part of the polluted political climate,” Davutoglu said in a statement.

The party currently has four seats in parliament. The party was established in 2019 with high hopes and entered parliament in 2023 thanks to a political alliance with the main opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP.

However, it failed to become a popular choice among conservative and Islamist voters, who are seen as the bastion of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP.

According to Davutoglu, his party tried to gather conservative forces together but did not succeed.

“From the outset, we sought to unite this new group internally first and then, if possible, merge it with the other conservative parties into a single party. Where that was not possible, we aimed to build a close, organic alliance. However, those efforts were ultimately unsuccessful,” he said.

Davutoglu was an architect of an AKP foreign policy that has seen Turkey extend its influence across the former Ottoman lands of the Balkans and the Middle East.

Known as the policy of “zero problems with neighbours”, Davutoglu developed the strategy while working as a professor of international relations at institutions including the prestigious Malaysian Islamic University.

In 2003, he was appointed an ambassador by then Prime Minister Abdullah Gul before going on to become chief foreign policy advisor to Gul’s successor, Erdogan, and then foreign minister in 2009.

The neighbourhood policy was outlined in his 2001 book, Strategic Depth, which advocated greater Turkish engagement and influence in the region, focusing on the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Central Asia.

His star rose when he was appointed prime minister in 2014, when Erdogan moved into the presidency. But a number of disagreements between the two and Davutoglu’s efforts to play a more visible role in domestic and foreign policy led to his resignation in 2016, under pressure from Erdogan. He finally resigned from the AKP in 2019.

Davutoglu saw the Balkans as a “natural and historical hinterland” for Turkish foreign policy given the strong bonds forged through centuries of Ottoman domination.

His promotion of Turkish ‘soft power’ saw the growth of government-backed bodies such as the Turkish aid agency, TIKA, the Yunus Emre cultural institutes, Turkish universities in the Balkans, media outlets and the Turkish Religious Authority, Diyanet.

Davutoglu founded the Future Party mainly with former AKP figures in a bid to challenge the President. According to recent opinion polls, however, the party had lost support.

The four Future Party MPs are expected to join the AKP or remain independent in parliament.

Despite his fading career in politics, Davutoglu still sounded a proud note. “This is not a decision of surrender. It is a decision to draw a moral line. This is not an abandonment of politics; it is a call for everyone to rethink politics.” Davutoglu wrote.

World.title: Hungary Enters Post-Print Age as Political Dailies Disappear
World.content:
End of an era

Urban believes that printed political newspapers could survive for another decade or so in larger European countries, but in smaller markets they are fast becoming an unsustainable business. Printing and distribution costs simply cannot compete with the economics of online publishing.

“Hungary is once again a pioneer, partly because the Orban government captured much of the media market,” Urban says. “It took control of most publishing houses and kept them afloat through state advertising and politically motivated advertising contracts.”

But as their content became more ideological and one-sided, readers deserted them. Most established media brands have now lost their credibility to such an extent that they can no longer sustain themselves on the competitive market or rely on subscriptions.

Nepszava’s story is somewhat different. Although it has been a consistent critic of the Orban government, it also relied – for the most part – on government advertising for the past four years. When Orban’s government lost power in the April 12 election, those revenues evaporated overnight.

“The journalists at Nepszava clearly produced critical reporting on the government,” Urban admits. “But, unfortunately, the company behind the newspaper was not financially independent from the state.”

Now struggling to survive as an online-only publication, Nepszava is finding that competition in the digital market is fierce. “We are in a lose-lose situation,” admits Nepszava’s Horvath. “Without a print edition, we have lost our subscribers. We don’t have s either. So, at the moment, we have no revenue at all.”

Both Nepszava and Magyar Nemzet have fallen well behind their competitors in the online news market. During the Orban years, many of Hungary’s independent media outlets reinvented themselves as online platforms and managed to develop sustainable business models while maintaining editorial independence. Many operate behind paywalls and most receive some EU grant funding, while traditional advertising has only slowly returned – if at all.

Magyar Hang, for example, a critical weekly newspaper, was forced to find a printing house in Slovakia when its business was turned away by a printing and distribution sector consolidated in the hands of Orban allies, but this helped the paper maintain its independence.

“Being online became a kind of guarantee of independence, while most of the print media was captured,” Urban points out.

The consequence is that many of the media outlets that were close to Orban’s government now find themselves on the brink following the April election. Regional newspapers, once an important source of information (disinformation, critics would argue) outside of Budapest and pillars of local communities, are also being converted into weeklies by August 1. Some pro-government outlets such as the tabloid Bors have already been closed, while others are making major layoffs. The weekly Mandiner, which also has a strong online presence, has reportedly laid off more than half its staff.

Some wonder how historians will evaluate this period in Hungary 50 or 100 years from now if no printed archives remain. In theory, the information will survive online, but all it takes is for someone to flick a switch for an archive to become inaccessible.

“It is a legitimate concern that online news could simply disappear if the servers are shut down,” Urban warns. “That would mean that stories, investigations and entire archives of media content could become inaccessible.”

Still, she believes there is no way back for print dailies. Weekly publications, offering more in-depth reporting, interviews and features, may still have a future, but online media is simply unbeatable when it comes to breaking news.

“This is another trend where Hungary is, sadly, once again a trendsetter,” Urban says. “But sooner or later, the rest of Europe will follow.”

World.title: Romania’s Farmers Feel the Heat as River Danube Dries Up
World.content:
The Danube is a vital European transport route for goods such as cereals, construction materials and fuel products, including exports from Ukraine.

In 2023, freight transport on the navigable stretch of the Danube between Germany and the Black Sea reached 55.2 million tonnes, according to the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine. The summer season is one of the busiest periods of the year, including for Ukrainian grain exports.

In southern Romania, much of the agricultural production transported along the Danube is shipped to the Black Sea port of Constanta.

But with the current restrictions, many farmers cannot sell their crops according to existing contracts. Daniel Nica, a farmer from Macesul de Jos, has 20,000 tonnes of wheat, barley and rapeseed stored in his silos, awaiting transport on the Danube.

“When we harvest the maize, we won’t have enough storage space,” he explained.

Like many farmers in the area, he usually sells to traders using the small port of Bechet. His company farms around 10,000 hectares of land in Dolj County, of which 2,500 hectares of maize are irrigated. Since early July, the irrigation canals supplied with water pumped from the Danube have dried out completely.

For Romanian farmers, such restrictions have become increasingly common in recent years. Coupled with repeated droughts, the lack of water availability is putting pressure on agriculture in Romania, one of the European Union’s largest agricultural producers and exporters of cereals.

This year, Romanian farmers have reported better rainfall than during previous summers, when some farmers reported total crop losses. But concerns remain over the longer term, especially for smaller producers.

Mugurel Ionut Stancu drives us through endless fields of sunflowers and maize, alongside a completely dried-up irrigation canal.

“Maize is currently at the stage when it needs the most water, as the kernels are filling. Without sufficient water supply, this will inevitably lead to lower yields and reduced quality,” he said.

Stancu joined the family farming business inspired by his grandfather, who had been cultivating land in the Valea Stanciului area, around 30 kilometres north of the Danube. Here too, farmers rely on water pumped from the river. Stancu’s family now farms 300 hectares, 58 of which have been irrigated since 2021.

“The need for irrigation emerged because droughts were persisting year after year, and spring crops, particularly maize and sunflower, were simply no longer profitable,” he recalled.

But lack of water availability could mean that this investment will take far longer than expected to pay off.

To increase the flow of water into the irrigation canals, authorities are dredging parts of the Danube to raise the water levels near pumping stations. Along the river, similar operations are being carried out to widen navigation channels for commercial barges.

“We began dredging works as early as April. The operations were divided into three sections, and a total of 270,000 cubic metres of sediments were dredged,” outlined Adrian Maizel from the Lower Danube River Administration.

But some experts fear these measures will not solve the problem in the long term.

“Dredging could lead to even lower groundwater levels,” warned Camelia Ionescu, who heads the water and climate project for WWF Romania, a nature protection campaign organisation.

Communist policies also to blame

World.title: Media Changes in Montenegro Intensify Alarm About Foreign Influence
World.content:
As Montenegro enters the final stage of its European Union accession process, concerns over harmful foreign influence are returning to the centre of public debate.

Experts are warning that media ownership changes, disinformation campaigns and political interference could all test the country’s democratic resilience ahead of elections expected in 2027.

The debate has intensified after a series of ownership changes and planned acquisitions involving some of Montenegro’s most influential media outlets, raising questions over the future of media pluralism and editorial independence in a country seeking to complete its EU path.

Both the European Commission and European Parliament have warned Montenegro about foreign interference, hybrid threats and information manipulation.

World.title: Two Greek Firefighters Die Battling Wildfire on Crete
World.content:
Two firefighters have died while battling a forest fire in the Krya Vrisi area of ​​Rethymno, on the island of Crete, the Greek Fire Service announced on Wednesday. State television reported that one was a seasonal firefighter and the other was a five-year veteran. They were reportedly trapped in their vehicle in the flames.

The Fire Service expressed its condolences to the families and loved ones of the deceased in a statement issued on Wednesday: “They fell heroically in the line of duty to protect the lives and property of citizens and the natural environment.”

The fire in Rethymno started in a forest area due to strong winds. Currently, 110 firefighters are operating on the front in six groups on the ground, with 27 vehicles, four helicopters as well as water tankers.

Strong winds are blowing in the area. Emergency messages have been sent to nearby residents to evacuate their homes. The villages of Krya Vrysi, Saktouria and Melampes have already been evacuated.

The Rethymno Arson Investigation Unit is investigating the causes of the fire.

Wildfires have also broken out in Messinia and Laconia in the Peloponnese and on the island of Mytilene, in the North Aegean.

A fire broke out on Tuesday on the island of Paros, in the Cyclades, which was brought under control – but a battle is still being fought to prevent a resurgence.

World.title: How Can Sweden Have Cheaper Petrol Than Croatia With No Domestic Production?
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Sweden produces almost no domestic oil, yet drivers there usually have access to much cheaper petrol than Croatia. How is that possible? The answer is more complex than you might realise.

The answer to the question posed above is that fuel prices are not simply determined by whether a country has oil reserves. Slobodan Mufic explained for Index that the final price at the pump depends on a combination of factors, including taxes, government decisions, competition between fuel companies, transport costs and market conditions.

Sweden imports the oil that it needs, but it has an incredibly highly developed energy market and strong purchasing power. The country has also introduced policies that influence the cost structure of fuels and energy, meaning the absence of domestic oil production does not automatically lead to higher prices. Croatia, meanwhile, also relies heavily on imported oil, but fuel prices are shaped by different economic conditions. The Croatian government has repeatedly intervened in the fuel market by setting maximum retail prices and adjusting measures such as excise duties to protect consumers from price increases.

Another important factor is the difference in wages. A litre of petrol may cost a similar amount across Europe, but what matters for citizens is how much of their income goes towards filling up their cars.

The comparison between Sweden and Croatia shows that having domestic oil production is not the only factor that determines fuel prices. Countries without their own oil can still have cheaper petrol if their tax systems, markets and economic conditions create lower costs for drivers. So while Croatia and Sweden both depend on imported energy, the price drivers behind the pump are much more complicated than simply asking: “Who has oil?”

World.title: Croatia’s Greatest Strength is Outstanding English Skills Says Global Study
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Croatia’s greatest strength is the outstanding English skills of its population, according to a recently commissioned global outsourcing study.

Croatia’s strongest competitive advantage on the global outsourcing market is its exceptional command of the English language, according to the 2026 Global Talent Index for Outsourcing published by the U.S. consulting company Ataraxis. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that the study assessed 193 UN-recognised countries using five key criteria: labour costs, English proficiency, talent availability, digital infrastructure and political stability.

The report highlights Croatia as one of the emerging success stories in Europe’s outsourcing industry, which is worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually and is no longer dominated solely by traditional outsourcing hubs such as India and the Philippines. Eastern European countries are becoming increasingly competitive, with Croatia standing out as a “hidden gem” in the European market.

croatia’s english skills see it receive 100 out of 100

According to the study, Croatia is one of only two countries in Eastern Europe, alongside Romania, to achieve a perfect score of 100 out of 100 for English proficiency. This places Croatia alongside native English-speaking countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States and South Africa, giving it a significant advantage when competing for international business.

The report notes that strong English skills are only part of Croatia’s appeal. The country also scored 90 out of 100 for digital infrastructure and 84 out of 100 for labour costs, creating a balanced profile that is attractive to companies looking to outsource high-value work. Croatia is home to almost 70,000 technology professionals, providing a solid foundation for further growth in the sector.

500 new croatian ict companies are established yearly

The country’s technology industry is also expanding rapidly. According to HUP-ICT, around 500 new ICT companies are established in Croatia every year, making it one of the most dynamic parts of the national economy.

Croatia’s digital infrastructure also compares favourably with the rest of Europe. The country has 82.7% coverage of very high-capacity broadband networks, 77.9% fibre-to-the-premises coverage, and 97.8% 5G network coverage, placing it above the European average in several key categories. These factors strengthen Croatia’s position as an attractive destination for international companies seeking outsourcing partners.

The Ataraxis report concludes that Croatia’s combination of excellent English proficiency, competitive labour costs, strong digital infrastructure and a growing technology sector gives it a unique opportunity to attract more international outsourcing projects and strengthen its position in the global digital economy.
