“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Amy V. Diaz appointed Chargé d’Affaires at US Embassy in Georgia
World.content:
The US Embassy has announced that Amy V. Diaz has been appointed Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Georgia. The announcement was published on the embassy’s official website.

According to the embassy, Diaz is a senior career member of the US Foreign Service and has served in the role since July 2026.

Who is Amy V. Diaz?

Amy V. Diaz has held a range of diplomatic and leadership positions throughout her career. Before her current appointment, she served as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim and Deputy Chief of Mission at the US Embassy in Lilongwe, Malawi.

Earlier, she worked at the US State Department’s Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs, where she was Deputy Director of the Office of Policy and Global Issues.

Diaz also headed the consular section at the US Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, and led the counternarcotics team at the US Embassy in Afghanistan.

Her previous assignments also include serving as rule of law adviser and coordinator for the Summit of the Americas at the US Embassy in Panama, chief of the internal political unit at the US Embassy in Tbilisi, and vice consul at US diplomatic missions in Harare and Monterrey, Mexico.

US Chargé d’Affaires ad interim to Georgia Amy W. Diaz

Diaz joined the US State Department in 2002 through the Presidential Management Fellows programme and has been a career member of the US Foreign Service since 2005.

She holds a bachelor’s degree from St. John’s College in Annapolis, Maryland, and a Juris Doctor degree from the University of Arizona. According to the State Department, she has received multiple Superior Honor Awards and Meritorious Honor Awards in recognition of her distinguished service.

The post of US ambassador to Georgia has remained vacant since July 2025, when Robin Dunnigan stepped down. Since then, the embassy has been headed by a series of Chargés d’Affaires ad interim. Alan Purcell initially led the mission, before Amy W. Diaz was appointed US Chargé d’Affaires ad interim to Georgia in July 2026. Washington has yet to nominate a new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the country.

Amy W. Diaz named acting US envoy to Georgia

World.title: Foreign visitor numbers and tourism revenue decline in Georgia
World.content:
The number of foreign visitors to Georgia and the country’s tourism revenue both declined in the second quarter of 2026, although visitor satisfaction and the average length of stay increased, according to a new report by the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat).

Official data show that 1.3 million foreign visitors travelled to Georgia between April and June, down 5.2% compared with the same period in 2025.

Most visitors — 81.5% — were tourists, meaning they stayed in Georgia for at least one night. Same-day visitors accounted for 14.8%, while 3.8% made both same-day and overnight visits.

According to the statistics, neighbouring countries continued to account for the largest share of international visitors to Georgia. Russia remained the biggest source market, with 328,900 visitors, or 25.1% of the total. It was followed by Turkey (16.9%) and Armenia (10.8%).

The largest age group among visitors was people aged 31 to 50, who accounted for 45.6% of the total. Men made up 57.1% of visitors, while women accounted for 42.9%.

Nearly half of all visits to Georgia (49.6%) were made for holidays, leisure and recreation. Visiting friends and relatives accounted for 25.6% of trips, while 12% were made for transit purposes.

Tbilisi and the Adjara region remained the most popular destinations. The capital accounted for 36.9% of all visits, while Adjara attracted 26.2%.

The decline in visitor numbers was reflected in tourism revenue. According to Geostat, foreign visitors spent a total of 3 billion lari (around $1.11 billion) in Georgia during the second quarter of 2026, down 13.3% compared with the same period last year.

Average spending per visit also fell by 9.2% over the same period, to 1,922.1 lari (around $711.9). Visitors spent the largest share of their budgets on food and drinks (27.3%), shopping (25.2%) and accommodation (24.3%).

Despite the decline in both visitor numbers and tourism spending, foreign visitors continued to rate their experience in Georgia highly. Some 54.4% of respondents described their trip as “very satisfying”, while 38.7% said it was “satisfying”, bringing the combined satisfaction rate to 93.1%.

The Geostat report also showed that the average length of stay increased from 5.30 to 5.48 nights. Meanwhile, 81.8% of visits were made by repeat visitors, indicating that most foreign travellers who have visited Georgia at least once return to the country.

Tourism in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi to demolish landmark Rike Jugs complex
World.content:
The landmark Rike Jugs architectural complex in central Tbilisi, on Europe Square, is being demolished after the city authorities granted permission for the work.

The site, which has remained unused for nearly 15 years, will be redeveloped into a hotel. Most of Rike Park — an area of around 15,000 square metres — will now pass into private ownership.

The complex, known as the Rike Jugs, consists of a music theatre and an exhibition centre. It was built in 2011–2012 in one of the busiest tourist areas of the Georgian capital. The project was conceived by then-President Mikheil Saakashvili and designed by Italian architect Massimiliano Fuksas.

The complex was never used for its intended purpose. Construction was completed just as power changed hands in Georgia, and the new ruling Georgian Dream party took a dim view of the Rike Jugs, along with other architectural projects associated with the Saakashvili era. Party members described the complex as a “dump” and said it was an eyesore.

After years of standing empty, the Rike Jugs were eventually put up for sale. Several auctions failed before the complex was sold in 2022 for 10 million lari (about $3.7 million) to businessman David Khidasheli, an associate of Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili. After Khidasheli’s relationship with the authorities deteriorated — leading to the loss of parts of his business and several licences — he decided to sell the property.

The complex changed hands again in 2025, when it was acquired by Rike Domi, a company registered on 25 April that year.

Under the terms of the deal, the company must build a hotel on the site by 2030, investing 44 million lari (around $16.3 million) in the project.

Urban planning experts and anti-corruption researchers say the sale bears signs of corruption. They argue the complex was sold for well below the market value of comparable property in Tbilisi, particularly in a prime tourist area in the city centre. When it was first offered at auction, the asking price for the Rike Jugs was 95 million lari (about $35.2 million)..

Tbilisi demolishes Rike Jugs complex

World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Young Indigenous creators dealing with social media 'cesspit'
World.content:
Katlyn Yeeda started sharing her love of fishing on social media more than a decade ago.

The Warrwa woman, known online as the Derby Jetty Queen, never thought casting a line would generate hundreds of hateful comments.

But simple posts featuring Ms Yeeda's latest catches were met with racist abuse.

"I didn't realise how bad it [racism] was on social media," she said.

"With all the hate comments I thought … 'I don't want to do this'."

Everyday posts of Katlyn Yeeda fishing from the horseshoe jetty were met with abuse online. (Supplied: Katlyn Yeeda)

Ms Yeeda grew up fishing with her family in Derby, 2,000km north of Perth in Western Australia's Kimberley.

Her expertise from the horseshoe jetty has attracted nationwide support, and helped to put positive stories of her home town on the map.

"Everyone loved what I was doing," Ms Yeeda said.

" They came up to me and told me they loved seeing someone from our own town getting out there and showing what Derby is. "

Ms Yeeda says she was determined not to let racist comments stop her from posting to social media. (Supplied: Katlyn Yeeda)

Ms Yeeda said racist comments had made her reconsider posting to social media.

"There's down days where I'm like, 'I'm so over it, I just want to give up'," she said.

But Ms Yeeda said she was determined not to allow the comments — many of which drew upon harmful stereotypes — to stop her from posting.

"I realised, this is what they want," she said.

"They don't want us to put our lifestyle out there and show how we're living a different lifestyle from them."

Hatred 'getting worse'

It's an all-too familiar story for Darwin chef Zach Green.

Born in Melbourne, Mr Green is a descendant of the Gunditjmara people in south-west Victoria.

The 37-year-old said he first experienced online racism and abuse when he started posting to social media as The Story Teller Chef in 2018.

His content focused on celebrating culture through Indigenous recipes and stories.

But the trolling and abuse had nothing to do with the food he was sharing on camera.

Gunditjmara man and chef Zach Green celebrates Indigenous culture through cooking. (Supplied: Zach Green)

"It was very confronting and I didn't understand it," Mr Green said.

"Why people would say those horrible, racist things, especially when I was just trying to cook food that was grown in our own backyard."

After taking a break from social media platforms for a couple of years, Mr Green has recently returned to his public profile.

"I'm a bit more resilient in not reading the comments and blocking people," he said.

" But at the same time I think it's just got worse … it does take a toll. "

Mr Green said he did not believe social media platforms were "really protecting anyone at this time".

"How can someone that isn't from that culture make the justification that something should be blocked or reported when they haven't lived the culture before?" he said.

Inquiry highlights online racism

Mr Green and Ms Yeeda's experience has been echoed in a national inquiry probing the extent of racism against Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

Australia's Human Rights Commission and Indigenous advocacy groups told the inquiry online hatred against Indigenous Australians had increased since the failed 2023 Voice to Parliament referendum.

The University of Technology Sydney's Jumbunna Institute for Indigenous Education and Research was amongst those who made submissions.

In 2022, the institute developed a Call it Out register to record instances of racism towards First Nations people across Australia.

Dr Allison says the lack of regulation on social media platforms was "really problematic". (Supplied: Fiona Allison)

Associate professor Fiona Allison said social media acted as a "cesspit" for harmful stereotypes.

"The platforms themselves are doing so little to address it," she said.

With the influence of politics and lack of regulation, Dr Allison predicted it was only going to become more of an issue in future.

Jody Nunn says online hatred was creating a "deep social divide". (Supplied: Jody Nunn)

Reconciliation WA chief executive Jody Nunn said the organisation's latest national data from 2024 showed a third of First Nations people had experienced racism online in the past six months.

"They're pretty startling statistics," she said.

" That level of hate speech and racism is causing deep social divide. "

Meta defends regulatory policies

At a Brisbane hearing of the inquiry held this week, Meta was accused of failing to respond effectively to anti-Indigenous content.

Meta representatives defended the company and told the inquiry the company had created an advisory group to combat hate, which included people from First Nations communities.

The representatives said they did not believe there were any Indigenous Australians employed as content moderators.

World.title: Unions confirm new 24-hour strike against BHP
World.content:
BHP is facing renewed industrial action in Western Australia's Pilbara, with unions lodging notice of a 24-hour strike against the mining giant.

Unions representing workers at BHP's operations in Port Hedland have lodged notice with the Fair Work Commission of the day-long action.

Members of the combined Ports Unions — the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), the Australian Manufacturing Workers Union (AMWU) and the Australian Workers Union (AWU) — will down tools on August 9 from 5:30am if a renewed bargaining meeting scheduled for next week fails to result in an agreement.

A 24-hour ban on loading ships will take place the day before.

Unions inflated this protest balloon, "Scabby the Cat", outside the port during the previous strike. (ABC Pilbara: Andrew Seabourne)

Unions said the planned action followed "glacial progress" in bargaining discussions between workers and the company in recent weeks.

An eight-hour strike on July 16 attracted about 100 workers, union staff and supporters.

But it resulted in minimal disruption to BHP's port operations, with seven ships loaded during the stoppage.

Union representatives said the miner had plenty of opportunities to avoid another strike.

"Despite our members negotiating for months, BHP continues to refuse to put forward an agreement that reflects the workers each day," AMWU WA secretary Steve McCartney said.

"This action is the direct result of the company's failure to negotiate seriously."

Steve McCartney speaks to ETU national secretary Michael Wright at the Port Hedland strike in July. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

ETU WA secretary Adam Woodage said BHP's proposal was not "fair or transparent".

"The people who enable this company's exorbitant profits are sending a message with this action: We want an honest deal, in black and white, and we are not going to entertain what the company is pushing," he said.

BHP has described the strike action as "disappointing" and has asked the Fair Work Commission (FWC) to oversee a negotiated outcome.

"BHP is frustrated by the lack of progress in bargaining and concerned about the lack of genuine engagement from the unions in bargaining meetings," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"We have shared our concerns directly with the union and asked them to provide greater clarity and detail around what they are proposing.

"Should we need to, we will seek further assistance from the Fair Work Commission to ensure we can reach a fair and reasonable agreement as quickly as possible."

Warning of threat to economy

The latest notification comes after unions and BHP again failed to agree at Tuesday's bargaining meeting.

The meeting did not include the participation of the FWC, although it is expected the next bargaining meeting, scheduled for next Tuesday, will be before the commission.

BHP's Port Hedland operations handle millions of dollars worth of iron ore exports each week. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

The strikes have prompted criticism from WA's Chamber of Minerals and Energy, which has described the return of industrial action to the Pilbara as a threat to the national economy.

Millions of dollars worth of iron ore leave Port Hedland each week, with a 24-hour stoppage potentially costing BHP $120 million in lost revenue, and the WA government $6.85 million in royalty payments.

A poll commissioned by the ETU and released earlier this week claimed the majority of voters supported workers at the port who took industrial action.

The survey of 1,503 people, conducted by YouGov, found 71 per cent supported workers taking strike action at Port Hedland.

World.title: Live: US stocks lift and ASX 200 set to follow
World.content:
Lots. Here's a summary

Microsoft jumps 15.5% after forecasting sales and cloud growth above expectations

30-year US Treasury yield reaches 5.2444%, highest level since mid-2007

Yen rallies 2.53% to 159.34 per US dollar, sparking intervention speculation

Tech shares lead rally, after recent declines on AI-spending worries

US stocks rallied on Thursday, led by Microsoft's 15.5% surge, while 30-year Treasury yields scaled a 19-year peak after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on Wednesday unsettled investors, concerned that the Fed would be insufficiently vigilant about long-term inflation.

The yen also gained sharply, prompting speculation that Japanese officials intervened to shore up the beleaguered currency.

Tech giant Microsoft carried the chip sector on its back after exceeded expectations for current-quarter sales and cloud growth and said coming capital expenditures would be less than what Wall Street anticipated. It also said it expects to keep generating cash through the just-started fiscal 2027.

Investors have been rattled by rising AI costs at big technology firms even as they report strong earnings. Negative cash-flow reports from Google's parent company Alphabet and EV maker Tesla last week sparked a selloff in AI-linked stocks, with chip stocks also under pressure as investors questioned high valuations.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1.2% to 52,209.57, the S & P 500 gained 1.7% to 7,437.99 and the Nasdaq Composite was up 2.8% at 25,122.18.

Microsoft's rally added $450 billion in market value to the company, the largest one-day dollar gain in history.

"Microsoft delivered yesterday, and maybe Microsoft is going to be able to move itself from the 'battleground' camp to be a 'trusted AI winner' stock," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.

The MSCI All Country World Price index rose 1.6% after earlier falling to its lowest level since June 11.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index rose 0.8%.

South Korea's KOSPI fell 1.2% to end its third consecutive day of losses

Bond market hits yield record

Longer-dated Treasury yields extended Wednesday's sharp rise after the Fed's decision to hold interest rates steady raised fears that inflation — already running well above the Fed's target — could climb further.

The decision to leave policy on hold drew dissent votes from three of the 12 FOMC members, who had wanted a quarter-percentage-point hike instead. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's preference for less forward guidance has left traders even less certain of the Fed's next move.

Warsh noted that bond yields had risen notably since the Fed's last policy meeting, reflecting investors pricing in future rate increases. He welcomed that move, while adding that it did not mean the central bank needed to ratify it with action of its own.

Here's Thomas Urano, co-chief investment officer at Sage Advisory in Austin, Texas:

"The strategy behind pulling back on forward guidance is forcing the market to take responsibility and enlisting the market in helping him do his job."

A recent uptick in oil prices pushed yields higher ahead of the Fed meeting, as fighting resumed in the US-Iran war. Fed funds futures traders are now pricing in 64% odds of a hike at the Fed's September meeting.

The interest-rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield rose 0.17 basis points to 4.238% while the yield on benchmark U.S. 10-year notes increased 4.51 basis points to 4.667%.

Thirty-year yields were last up 6.62 basis points at 5.2092% and reached 5.2444%, the highest since mid-2007.

Oil prices settled lower after a volititily, pulling back after a sharp few days of gains following the resumption of attacks between the U.S. and Iran.

Saudi Arabia has proposed plans for a maritime coalition to boost defense cooperation around the Red Sea. It is unlikely when a coalition would start to protect shipping.

US inflation slowed in June. with the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index rising 3.7% in the 12 months through June, after an unrevised 4.1% gain in May — the largest increase since April 2023.

US economic growth slowed too due to the widening trade deficit, though other factors, including accelerating consumer spending and robust business investment in AI infrastructure, pointed to underlying strength.

Intervention speculation on Yen

The Japanese yen rallied suddenly on Thursday, sparking speculation that Japanese authorities had stepped in to steady the currency after it weakened to a 40-year low against the US dollar.

“The further it falls the more likely intervention becomes as an explanation," said Nick Rees, head of macro research at Monex Europe.

"It’s a fairly sizeable fall and there’s no other obvious catalyst and the timing makes sense, coming at month-end and after weak U.S. data. Although we won’t know for certain for a while.”

The Bank of Japan is expected to keep rates steady at 1% on Friday. After raising rates in June, a second successive hike would be unusual.

The yen was last up 2.53% against the greenback at 159.34 per dollar.

The dollar index which measures the U.S. currency against a basket of peers including the yen and the euro, fell 0.84% to 99.94, with the euro up 0.57% at $1.153.

Sterling strengthened 0.73% to $1.3466.

The Bank of England kept interest rates on hold as expected, but a third policymaker backed a rate hike, citing renewed conflict between the United States and Iran.

Spot gold rose 1.11% to $4,110.19 an ounce.

- Reuters

World.title: Qld domestic violence minister blames former government for system failings
World.content:
Queensland's embattled domestic and family violence prevention minister has attempted to flip the script, claiming victims of family and domestic violence are "frightened" to seek support due to a "shameful scare campaign" about frontline service funding.

Amanda Camm made the sensational statements during a late-night budget estimates hearing on Thursday evening.

During estimates, the minister also defied a promise by the premier that she would provide an update on the progress of the implementation of recommendations from a taskforce set up to combat coercive control and domestic violence.

Domestic and Family Violence Minister Amanda Camm has faced scrutiny over both domestic violence funding and a rise in young children being held in residential care. (ABC News)

The minister has been under fire for weeks, with the Opposition calling for her to be sacked following reports $40 million was axed from the budget for domestic and family violence prevention.

The LNP has denied funding was stripped from frontline services, and saying the gap in the budget was for the women's safety and justice taskforce, which was "time-limited" and had been "delivered".

Minister Camm began her opening statement for the domestic and family violence prevention portfolio by saying Labor had orchestrated a "shameful," "perverse" "scare campaign" against her.

She said she had been contacted by several domestic violence victim-survivors, who told her they were now planning their own funerals and taking out life insurance "in the event that they were murdered at the hands of their perpetrator".

"Over the past week alone, several women have told us they are now even more frightened to seek support because they believe, based on what they are hearing on social media and in the media, that service will not be there when they need them," she told estimates.

On Thursday during estimates, Director-General Belinda Drew said $10.569 million had been re-allocated from domestic and family violence services to "other families initiatives".

Ms Drew said it was re-invested in financial counselling, emergency relief and other programs.

The state government has allocated $340.7 million towards DFV prevention in the 2026-27 financial year. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Minister refuses to table progress for landmark report

On July 19, Premier David Crisafulli promised media that Ms Camm would provide an update on the progress of the implementation of recommendations from reports by the women's safety and justice taskforce.

"I will ask the minister to update as part of the estimates process … I'll allow the minister to give you the exact numbers," Mr Crisafulli told media nearly a fortnight ago.

The taskforce made 277 recommendations to the state government across two reports handed down in 2021 and 2022.

On Thursday evening, Shadow Treasurer Shannon Fentiman came to collect that update, but was left wanting.

Despite Ms Fentiman repeatedly asking for Ms Camm to table the update, the minister did not.

In a response spanning 10 minutes, Ms Camm said her government had stood up a peak body for domestic and family violence and another for sexual violence.

"The premier promised an update, but the minister defied him by refusing time and time again to provide the status of all recommendations," Ms Fentiman said in a statement.

" It's about time the premier draws a line in the and removes this underperforming minister. "

Ms Camm did not respond to the ABC's request for a clear breakdown of the implementation of the recommendations, but during estimates said more had been done under her government than Labor.

Children in residential care in Qld higher than ever The Queensland government has handed down its response to the Child Safety Inquiry.

"We want to make sure that when we deliver upon these recommendations, that we're not just closing in them out and ticking a box, that we're actually going to evaluate them," Ms Camm told estimates.

Earlier in the evening, during the probe of the child safety portfolio, the committee heard more than 6400 child safety cases have not been investigated following an IT failure that put Queensland youth in state care at risk.

The bungled $183 million 'Unify' system — a platform which tracked the records of around 16 thousand children in state care — was put under the microscope last year, after it was revealed gaps in the program were putting children at risk.

Ms Drew revealed there was currently a backlog of 8,140 case assessments and 78 per cent had not been commenced as of June 30.

World.title: Luke Gosling facing growing calls to stand down after assault charges
World.content:
Questions remain over Labor Member for Solomon Luke Gosling's political future after he was arrested and charged with two counts of assault yesterday morning.

The charges relate to an incident involving Mr Gosling and Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly, the territory's equivalent of a state governor, at the NT Grand Thai Festival in Darwin on July 18.

Mr Gosling has been bailed to appear before the Darwin Local Court on September 1 and has strenuously denied the allegations against him.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has remained tight-lipped on Mr Gosling's future, saying it would be inappropriate to comment while the legal process is under way.

Anthony Albanese says it would be inappropriate to comment while the charges are before the court. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

But there are growing calls for Mr Gosling to step aside, with Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson urging Mr Albanese to stand him down as special envoy for defence, veterans' affairs and northern Australia.

"No-one should be serving in a ministerial or quasi-ministerial role while facing charges like those," he told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing.

"I make no judgement about Luke Gosling's guilt or innocence; he is entitled to the presumption of innocence, we should allow the legal process to follow, but in the meantime, he should stand down from that role."

Jacinta Nampijinpa Price says Luke Gosling's arrest on assault charges is "troubling". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

NT senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price said while it would be wrong to prejudge Mr Gosling, the prime minister needed to act.

"It is troubling that one of our community's elected leaders has been arrested in relation to an alleged assault on the king's representative in the territory," she said in a statement.

" Given the seriousness of the allegations, the prime minister should stand Mr Gosling aside from his special envoy responsibilities while the matter is investigated. "

Mr Gosling, a military veteran who has held the Darwin-based seat of Solomon for the past 10 years, has consistently maintained his innocence since the allegations first emerged last week.

Speaking outside Palmerston police station yesterday morning, Mr Gosling's lawyer, Marty Aust SC, said his client would contest the charges in court.

Marty Aust says his client denies any wrongdoing and will vigorously defend the charges. (Supplied: NT News/Julianne Osborne)

"The charge is completely and utterly denied and will be contested," he said.

In a post on Instagram, Mr Gosling wrote: "I can't say much because the matter is before the courts, but it's been a strange morning, to say the least.

"Anyway, we're all cracking on with it. I'll stay focused on doing my job and building a stronger Territory and better nation for all of us."

Mr Aust also raised doubts about the motivation behind the charges.

Police alleged Luke Gosling assaulted David Connolly (pictured) while both men were attending the Grand Thai Festival in Darwin earlier this month. (Supplied)

"It's particularly concerning that the police resorted to the power of arrest when they could have dealt with this matter by way of summons or notice to appear," he said.

"There's a real concern that there's a degree of politicisation in relation to how this matter is being handled already."

NT Police has denied the charges were in any way influenced by the public positions of the men involved.

"Allegations that the investigation has been politicised are without foundation," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Labor's political opponents say Luke Gosling should stand down until the charges are resolved. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Mr Gosling was one of three federal Labor politicians who criticised Mr Connolly earlier this year over his past social media posts which were labelled by some as "racist" and "denigrating of women".

Mr Connolly later apologised for the posts, a day before he was sworn into the vice-regal position.

Mixed precedent for political future

Senator Paterson said there was a precedent for members of parliament facing charges to stand down.

"In the previous parliament, under previous governments, people facing allegations that were historic in nature, that did not even amount to charges, let alone convictions, were required to resign from their positions," he said.

University of Sydney constitutional law professor Anne Twomey said the severity of the charges usually determined such actions.

Anne Twomey says MPs only lose their seats if convicted of certain offences, with an arrest alone not enough. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

"If what they've been accused of is offensive and on-the-nose, then [the government] might encourage them to leave the party or tell them they're gone," she said.

" It really depends on the nature of the charge. "

But she said there was no legal basis for Mr Gosling to lose his seat over the charges.

"It's not the arrest that would lead you to lose your seat; you would have to be tried and convicted," she said.

MP charged with assault Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been charged with assaulting NT Administrator David Connolly, the territory equivalent of a state governor, at a festival earlier this month.

Stephen Wilks, an academic researcher at the Australian National University's National Centre of Biography, said the precedent for politicians facing criminal charges was mixed.

"It's unusual for somebody who's really senior in politics, subject to credible allegations and even court proceedings, not to stand down, but it does happen," he said.

Dr Wilks said several factors would inform the decision on whether to stand Mr Gosling down.

"It's really a matter of weighing up, on the one hand, what is the damage to the party of having this person stick around against losing their services," he said.

"There may be some degree of trade-off there."

World.title: 'Never for sale': European nations vow World Cup boycott over FIFA plan
World.content:
European nations have agreed to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions in protest over president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in soccer's biggest tournament to private equity investors.

"UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions," the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of its 55 member nations.

On a seismic day in soccer politics, support in Asia and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) for FIFA and Mr Infantino was also shaken.

The next scheduled FIFA tournament is within weeks in Europe — the Women's Under-20 World Cup hosted by Poland from September 5 — and the four British federations comprise FIFA's only bidder to host the 2035 Women's World Cup. That decision is due November 23.

"Some things are simply too important to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

The strategy meeting was called to counter Mr Infantino's offer of $US20 million ($28.45 million) to each of FIFA's 211 global members that has to be accepted by mid-September.

Mr Infantino's secret project was revealed on Tuesday to spin off its commercial operations in a new $US20 billion ($28.45 billion) subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The core investor would be a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Mr Infantino wrote to the 211 members — already the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law — that if they approve FFE, their promised $US10 million basic funding for the next four years will double to $US20 million. He projected their FIFA funding through 2038 would be $US86 million ($122 million) each, instead of about $US36 million ($51 million).

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football," said UEFA, where Mr Infantino was a staffer and its CEO-like general secretary when he was first elected to lead FIFA in 2016.

Mr Infantino's high-stakes gambit now could threaten his previously secure 11-year presidency of FIFA as anger and frustration with him rise among soccer stakeholders, including three of the six continental bodies.

FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in a presidential vote of the 211 members scheduled next March in Rabat, Morocco.

Mr Infantino had seemed after the World Cup to have a clear path to being re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term in office through 2031, despite a furore over letting United States forward Folarin Balogun play against Belgium despite a red card in his previous game.

"Game over, Gianni #InfantinOUT," the Football Supporters Europe group, which advises UEFA on fan issues such as ticket prices, posted after the boycott threat.

UEFA detailed why soccer officials fear external investors owning a stake in the global game's biggest events, including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women.

"The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever," UEFA said. "Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure."

Mr Infantino has presented the private equity offer as a chance to "turbocharge" funding development of soccer across the world, where a majority of the 211 FIFA members rely on its funding.

Officials from about 40 UEFA members spoke at the urgent meeting, with anger expressed that FIFA is not using some of its multi-billion-dollar reserves to fund extra development programs.

"As a result of today's discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive," the European soccer body said, "unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership."

CONCACAF also released a statement saying its organisation was built on service, "transparent governance, and the long-term stewardship of football".

"History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values," it said.

Deep concerns were raised about the lack of due process, the short deadline imposed, the lack of review or approval by relevant bodies, and the need for private investment to fund programs.

"For these reasons, CONCACAF and its 41 Member Associations have rejected the proposal."

The associations called on their FIFA Council Members to engage FIFA to determine how existing FIFA reserves could be used to increase FIFA Forward funding for football development across our region, and urged that all matters follow proper governance processes.

CONCACAF did not threaten a boycott of FIFA competitions. However, Europe's 55 associations and CONCACAF's 41 would make nearly half of the 211 total votes available.

"FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football," the Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said in a letter to its 46 members of FIFA, warning of risks to their own competitions.

Sheikh Salman, an ally of Mr Infantino since losing the FIFA presidential election to him in 2016, wrote: "Such an initiative will not succeed without the support of all the confederations, which is not the case now."

In a video message published Wednesday by FIFA, Infantino insisted spinning off its money-making operations was "an offer, not an obligation."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

A FIFA presentation for its members, co-written with its banking advisors from J.P. Morgan and seen by the AP, set a goal for FFE as "commercial rigour and expertise to better capitalise on broadcast rights, sponsorships and a growing tournament portfolio."

That growing portfolio likely would include adding more teams to FIFA competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup for men and women, and potentially staging them more often than every four years, including in the U.S.

FIFA adding teams, games and competitions would squeeze the value, status and space in the congested global fixture calendar for those that fund and are organised by the six continental soccer bodies like UEFA and the AFC.

A threatened World Cup boycott from Europe helped derail Mr Infantino's plan in 2021 to play World Cups every two years instead of four.

AP/ABC

World.title: Council charges couples 'Noosa tax' to marry by the beach
World.content:
It seemed only natural for Jodie O'Dea and Daryl Pilmore to tie the knot at their favourite beach in Queensland's holiday hotspot — which they also call home.

"Getting married in Noosa was special to us," Ms O'Dea said.

"Even though the fees were quite high for the land, we were willing to book it given the sentimental significance and also being locals."

Daryl Pilmore and Jodie O'Dea lost their non-refundable permit fee after the council land became waterlogged. (Supplied: Jodie O'Dea)

Noosa Council charges a non-refundable $799 fee for a three-hour permit for the Noosa Main Beach foreshore area.

In the days leading up to the wedding in April, heavy rain caused the couple's ceremony site to become waterlogged.

"The day before we tried to get hold of the council to see if we could cancel that booking — we just couldn't reach anybody," Ms O'Dea said.

Maison La Plage is one of the wedding groves along Noosa's Main Beach foreshore. (Supplied: Lindy Yewen Photography)

They ended up having their ceremony at the reception venue, which cost an additional $3,000.

The council also did not refund their permit fee.

"I appreciate there are terms and conditions," Ms O'Dea said.

"Seventy of our 80 guests flew into Noosa for the wedding. They ate, shopped ... I did a kind of ballpark [figure] and I reckon we probably injected $50,000 to $80,000 into the local economy.

" A local resident can't even be afforded a goodwill gesture of a small refund for a piece of land that wasn't usable? "

A wedding ceremony being held on the Noosa Main Beach foreshore. (Supplied: Lindy Yewen Photography)

Love lost

The permit fee to marry along Noosa Main Beach has steadily risen over the years, from $159 in 2014 to $567.50 in 2020 — and now $799.

Rising price of weddings It's a premier location to get married, but are the council's rising fees deterring loved up couples?

It costs $399 to hold a wedding at all other locations the council manages, which has also jumped from $375 in 2025.

Lindy Yewen has worked as a wedding photographer in the region for more than 30 years.

She said couples were being driven away by the permit costs.

"They're paying high fees for accommodation. Dining is expensive here. So then you go and throw another $800 at them and it's off putting," Ms Yewen said.

" Our couples call it the Noosa tax. "

The Noosa Wedding Organisation says there has been a noticeable drop in weddings in recent years. (Supplied: Jacqueline Gray)

The Noosa Wedding Organisation, a not-for-profit group of local suppliers, found the number of ceremonies held in the region had dropped from 781 in 2014 to 563 in 2025.

"I think the permits is the main part of it, but I think another part is it's actually starting to feel unwelcoming," Ms Yewen said.

The organisation found the decline represented an estimated $30 million annual loss in visitor spending, with the average guest typically spending at least $2,600 during a three-day stay.

Celebrant Jacqueline Gray has been among industry members lobbying council to reduce its fees. (Supplied: Jacqueline Gray)

"Regardless of whether you've got anything to do with weddings, the accommodation, your cafes, restaurants, retail stores — all those people are going to miss out," Ms Yewen said.

Noosa wedding celebrant Jacqueline Gray said it was significantly cheaper to hold a wedding in the Sunshine Coast Council area, where there was a $83 flat fee.

"I do a number of weddings now in Point Arkwright and it's equally beautiful," she said.

She said she understood the council needed to recover its costs for administration fees and maintaining the public spaces, but claimed they were not always up to scratch.

"From what I've heard from couples, there are a lot of complaints made to council about the fee and about the state of the grassed area when they turn up," Ms Gray said.

" I've had families there with rakes and snippers, cleaning and blowing the area because it hasn't been done — just appalled at the state of the area they've paid so much money for. "

Local government area Beach permit Other areas Noosa Shire Council $799 (Main Beach) $399 Sunshine Coast Council $83 $83 Gold Coast Council Free $134-$345 Brisbane City Council n/a $218 Moreton Bay $165 $165 Port Douglas $150 (Little Cove) $76 Cairns $95 $95

A 'premium' price

Under the Local Government Act, councils are entitled to charge a "cost-recovery" fee to recoup any losses from facilitating ceremonies.

The fee can also include a tax if the council decides it will benefit the local government area.

In a statement, Noosa Council property manager Hayley Jamieson said the council welcomed weddings and recognised the "important contribution" they made to the local economy.

"The fee reflects the end-to-end costs associated with administering wedding permits ... compliance activities ... and a contribution towards the management and presentation of council-managed beaches, parks and foreshores," Ms Jamieson said.

"The higher fee applying to ceremonies within the Noosa Main Beach foreshore area reflects the premium nature of these locations, together with the higher level of management and presentation required."

The council said the fee was non-refundable, but in the event of severe weather officers would work with permit holders to accommodate requests to change ceremony times or locations on a "case-by-case" basis.

The Noosa Wedding Organisation is calling on the council to review its fees. (Supplied: Lindy Yewen Photography)

The fees are reviewed annually.

Ms Gray said she hoped the industry's pleas would be heard ahead of the next council budget.

"It's really impacting our Noosa brand. It's embarrassing," she said.

World.title: 'Momentous day' as Aboriginal ancestors' remains repatriated in Arnhem Land
World.content:
At a remote burial ground in Arnhem Land, nine Aboriginal ancestors have finally been laid to rest, following a rare and historic repatriation ceremony aimed at helping to heal the "wrongs of the past".

The remains of the Yolŋu ancestors were taken from the Northern Territory between 85 and 90 years ago by University of Melbourne anthropologist Donald Thomson.

In the decades since then, they had been sitting in a collection in Victoria, until new provenance research helped connect them back to their Arnhem Land communities.

Djambawa Marawili (left) says the ceremony is important to show younger generations "we can bring our ancestors back through the same song cycles and ceremonies of our forefathers". (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

By the waters of Blue Mud Bay in Bäniyala, the Maḏarrpa clan hosted a ceremony yesterday to mark the end of a years-long process to bring their ancestors home.

The ashes of the remains were placed in larrakitj (log coffins) and buried on top of a hill, a Christian cross above them, as the community's men sang the ancestral beings back onto their sacred land.

Maḏarrpa clan leader and renowned artist Djambawa Marawili, who was at the forefront of advocating for the repatriation, said it was a momentous day for Yolŋu people.

The ancestors' ashes were placed in traditional log coffins and buried on top of a hill. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"We need to show our young ones, so they know some of our ancestral heritage was taken away and stored on other people's country," he said.

" We need to show the future generations our culture has remained, and we can bring our ancestors back through the same song cycles and ceremonies of our forefathers. "

London museum returns Indigenous Australians' remains The remains of six Indigenous people are being returned to the Woppaburra, Warrgamay, Wuthathi, and Yadhighana communities in Queensland, and the traditional custodians of another 30 sets of remains are being identified.

Melbourne University Laureate Professor Marcia Langton, who has also been a long-term advocate for the repatriation of sacred and secret cultural objects, attended the Bäniyala ceremony and said the remains should never have been removed.

"The importance of returning ancestors and secret or sacred objects to clans and homelands cannot be underestimated," she said.

"They should not have been taken in the first place and have been held for too long in the so-called care of institutions, too far away from their families and clans."

Global push to return sacred objects

Melbourne University interim vice-chancellor Glyn Davis also called on institutions globally to follow suit in returning secret and sacred objects to their ancestral homes.

"The return of ancestors to country is a profound responsibility for universities and collecting institutions in Australia and worldwide," Professor Davis said.

Glyn Davis says the return of ancestors to country "is a profound responsibility for universities and collecting institutions". (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"Universities are now confronting the legacies of collecting practices centuries ago.

"We will work with communities for as long as necessary so ancestors and cultural heritage material can be returned to the places, families and custodians where they belong."

In a bid to get its message out to institutions around the world, the university will today send translated statements detailing the Bäniyala ceremony to institutions in the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, Denmark, Indonesia, Norway, Italy and the Czech Republic.

University stands by complex legacy

Melbourne University has held Aboriginal remains and sacred cultural objects in its collection since the 1870s, and is now in the process of trying to repatriate many of them to dozens of communities across Australia.

The university's deputy vice-chancellor (Indigenous), Barry Judd, said it was a chance to acknowledge "the wrongs of the past [and] to strengthen and heal for a better future".

Melbourne University has acknowledged the "great injustice" of the past practice of taking remains for study. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

Including the ceremony in Bäniyala, 14 ancestors have been returned to the Maḏarrpa, Dhaḻwaŋu, Djapu, Dhuḏi-Djapu, Marrakulu and Maŋgalili clans in north-east Arnhem Land over the past week.

The remains were all originally collected by renowned Australian anthropologist Donald Thomson.

Professor Thomson travelled widely in remote Arnhem Land, Far North Queensland and Central Australia in the first half of last century, as well as across the Pacific, to learn about the social lives of their remote residents.

The remains of the Yolŋu ancestors were taken from the Northern Territory between 85 and 90 years ago. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

The University of Melbourne has continued to pay its respects to Professor Thomson's legacy in academia and as a friend and advocate for Aboriginal people, while at the same time acknowledging his outdated practice of taking remains did a "great injustice" to impacted communities.

"The Donald Thomson Collection is of immense significance to Aboriginal peoples, and its value to researchers in Australia and internationally concerned with understanding human diversity cannot be underestimated," Professor Langton said.

Gilirryunmarrtji Marawili was among the Bäniyala men particicipating in the ceremony who were painted in gapan (clay). (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

Assembled by Professor Thomson at the university between 1928 and 1965, his collection comprised more than 10,000 objects, alongside photographs, films, audio recordings, field notes, journals, maps and natural science specimens.

World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic Transport CityCats out of action during peak, with commuters to be dropped off at nearest stop Julius Dennis Updated July 31, 2026 — 7:26am ,first published 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane ferry passengers will be dropped of at whichever stop is closest at 8am on Friday, with CityCat workers to take strike action for two of the service’s busiest hours. The strike comes as part of wider industrial action that will run for the week – through to Friday, August 7 – that will include cancelled services and ticketing equipment not being available. CityCats will stop running at whichever stop they are closest to at 8am. Julius Dennis Negotiations between the Australian Maritime Union and the boats’ operator, RiverCity Ferries, have fallen over, with unionists claiming they have been forced to take action. Services between 8am and 10am will be cancelled, with the vessels to progressively come back online after the action.



Signs posted by the council at terminals across the city say ferries will stop running at whichever stop they are closest to at 8am, with commuters urged to plan ahead to get to work on time. Related Article City council How much this retired CityCat sold for at auction “From 10am the services will resume progressively, with some delays expected while the network returns to normal,” the signs read. The Translink app is also displaying a warning about the action. A union spokesperson said 95 per cent of its members had voted against adopting the company’s latest pay and conditions offer.



“RiverCity Ferries won’t even match the Fair Work Commission’s own 4.75 per cent annual wage review increase or keep pace with inflation, claiming it is ‘not viable’ – all the while its parent company Kelsian Group’s own financial reports show substantial increases in revenue and profit,” the statement said. The signs have been posted at terminals around the city. Julius Dennis “The company’s CEO, executive leadership team and board have all received significant increases to their pay packages while our highly skilled and committed members that deliver the company’s service to the Brisbane public every day are being asked to accept an offer below inflation.” A RiverCity Ferries spokesperson said they were disappointed services would be disrupted. “We have been bargaining with the unions and employee representatives since October 2025 and remain committed to negotiating in good faith towards a fair and sustainable enterprise agreement,” they said.



“Our priority is to maintain safe and reliable ferry services wherever possible and minimise disruption to customers. We are working closely with Brisbane City Council and Translink to communicate any service impacts and to restore services as soon as possible.” A spokesperson for Transport and Main Roads said TMR is working with Brisbane City Council and RiverCity Ferries to minimise customer impacts. “This is a matter between RiverCity Ferries and their employees, and we encourage them to negotiate in good faith to reach an agreement as soon as possible.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe David Crowe Updated July 31, 2026 — 7:07am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of migrants have rushed across the border from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a startling move that was relayed on social media and triggered a political row about migration into Europe. One security official declared the border checkpoint had “totally collapsed” under pressure from the crowd, as young men spread instructions on social media on how to enter the Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa. Authorities said at least nine people had died trying to reach Ceuta from Morocco. Loading Some migrants swam from Moroccan territory to reach the Spanish enclave, while others walked around a breakwater and crossed the rocks in numbers that overwhelmed authorities. Spanish state television TVE reported that 2000 to 3000 people had crossed. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez promised an “immediate response” to the situation, as his critics blamed his migration laws for encouraging people to seek asylum in Spain and gain work rights in the European Union.



“We are mobilising all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible,” Sanchez said. Spain’s government later said it would send the military to help the Civil Guard “to maintain security in the city of Ceuta”. Thousands of people flood the border. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere The political impact reached far beyond Spain because of the debate across Europe about migration, with British right-wing leader Nigel Farage sharing the dramatic videos online.



“It’s time to wake up everybody,” Farage declared. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for urgent action and warned that her government might suspend an open-border passport agreement with Spain if the situation was not brought under control.



“The images coming from Ceuta are striking and demonstrate, once again, that uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe’s borders,” she said. “Italy will not stand by and watch. We are convening the relevant bodies, and following these meetings, we are prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain.” Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Civil Guard officers had to open the gates because they needed to prevent a bottleneck forming at the checkpoint.



Why are people fleeing Morocco? The rush follows a Supreme Court decision in Spain last month that protects migrants who are intercepted at sea while seeking to get to Ceuta, preventing them from being immediately returned to Morocco. That ruling is being blamed by some politicians for giving Moroccans an incentive to swim to Ceuta, a distance of about 2 kilometres across the water, or walk around the breakwater. There were chaotic scenes on the Ceuta shoreline. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Spanish police officers respond as migrants cross from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere



Another source of debate is the Sanchez government’s decision this year to grant an amnesty to migrants who were already in the country, leading to more than 1.3 million people applying to stay permanently. Ceuta, located roughly opposite Gibraltar in the western Mediterranean, has been a Spanish territory since 1580 and now has the status of an autonomous city of Spain, although it is surrounded by Moroccan territory. Spanish soldiers travel in military vehicles after being deployed to Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Rachid Sbihi, the head of the association that represents the Spanish Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, called for a national emergency to be declared in Madrid to stop the mass movement because the border had totally collapsed. “The situation is absolute chaos,” he said. “It’s not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing.”



The Ministry of the Interior in Madrid has pushed back at the idea of a national emergency being declared. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is due to travel to Ceuta on Friday. Migrants at the border of Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere The Mayor-President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the influx had overwhelmed the city’s ⁠reception system and left hundreds of migrants sleeping outside. “We are facing a situation ​of absolute humanitarian and social emergency,” Vivas told radio station Cadena SER, adding that facilities for ​unaccompanied minors were operating at 2400 per cent of capacity.



In comments to radio station Onda Cero, he described the situation as a national emergency and called for a “decisive, forceful, immediate and co-ordinated” response under a ​single command structure. Arrivals were currently averaging about 300 people a day, according to Vivas. At that pace, he warned, Ceuta could face a situation comparable to the May 2021 migration crisis, when 10,000 people entered ​the enclave in mere ​days. Belongings left behind by migrants float in the sea. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Vivas also pointed ⁠to the human cost of the crossings, saying 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months, and argued that ​stronger migration controls would help prevent further deaths.
