The federal government is trying to stop a loophole in the NDIS that allows providers to claim for unproven therapies including wellness treatments and animal therapy.

Jenny McAllister, the federal minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme, has just been speaking on ABC Radio National.

She has told AM host Sally Sara that people had used the loophole to claim golf lessons.

“This is totally inappropriate. We’re cracking down on this through a number of means: changing the price guide, increasing our analytic capability, and seeking support from the parliament for new powers so we can continue to investigate providers who are doing the wrong thing.

“We made it very clear in 2024 that therapy needs to be delivered by a qualified practitioner, and that wellness supports or alternative therapies are not suitable.”

The loophole has existed since 2019 – but McAllister said when Labor had come into government, they were told the body administering the NDIA had “essentially no compliance mechanisms built into the NDIA by the Liberals”.

World.title: ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge Stan Choe Updated July 31, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A monster day for Microsoft’s stock following signals that its big spending on AI is translating into profits led a powerful rebound on Wall Street, while computer-chip companies regained some of their sharp recent losses. In the bond market, though, worries remained about inflation potentially remaining high for years. The S&P 500 rallied 1.7 per cent and more than recovered its drop from the day before, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 613 points, or 1.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, rallied 2.8 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a gain of 110 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. On Wall Street, Microsoft led the way and leaped 15.5 per cent for its best day in nearly 18 years after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Apple released its results after the closing bell, with sales and profits beating Wall Street expectations, fuelled by its customers snapping up iPhones and MacBooks amid price increases across the consumer electronics sector. Driving Apple’s results was a 21.7 per cent increase in iPhone sales to $US54.25 billion ($77.2 billion), above analyst estimates of $US53.86 billion, according to LSEG data. Those iPhone sales were Apple’s best-ever for a third quarter, when phone sales typically begin to slow as customers anticipate new models during the fall. Apple shares are 3.3 per cent lower in after-hours trade. Meta Platforms fell 8 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year.



Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying to power their AI efforts rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. Micron Technology jumped 18.4 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5 per cent. It was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft. Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 18 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13 per cent. On the losing end of Wall Street was Jersey Mike’s Subs. The sandwich chain’s stock fell 6 per cent in its first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. All told, the S&P 500 rose 121.48 to 7,437.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 613.92 to 52,208.06, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 679.24 to 25,122.18.



In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 4.67 per cent, the same as late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield ticked up to 5.22 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. Those yields move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite inflation remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.



“If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate. Reports released Thursday suggested the U.S. economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May’s level. In the oil market, prices eased. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to settle at $US86.88 per barrel.



It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. Seoul’s market has been at the centre of AI’s huge swings because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.title: Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Billie Eder July 31, 2026 — 6:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scroll down for a complete Commonwealth Games medal tally Glasgow: Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was flicking through her local newspaper in Tasmania in 2021 when she saw an  for a cycling talent search. Bored at home during the COVID-19 pandemic, she thought, why not show up and give it a crack? Five years on, Wilson-Haffenden is a Commonwealth Games champion after motoring home to win gold in the women’s team pursuit alongside Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks and Alyssa Polites after only starting the sport in 2021. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images



“I don’t think I can say this too loudly because COVID probably wasn’t great for a lot of people. But for me, it changed my life,” Wilson-Haffenden said. “I can’t be grateful for COVID, but I can be grateful for the outcome, that’s for sure.” Wilson-Haffenden, who was a hockey player at the time, was lucky to make it at all – she had to call in a favour and delay her tryout. “I actually couldn’t make it on the talent ID date, and called saying ‘I really want to give this a crack’,” she said. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images



“So they made a little allowance for me, but I just think it’s a message to all young kids, if you’re interested, give it a crack because you never know where it’ll take you.” She now spends most of the year in Girona – a cycling town in Catalonia, in the north-east of Spain – but said it was her formative cycling years in Tasmania that turned her into a champion. “I actually think it’s the cold mornings in Tassie that really build character – I think G [teammate Georgia Baker] will attest to it as well,” Wilson-Haffenden said. Tara Neyland broke a world record on her way to winning gold. Getty Images “It’s a pretty lonely sport. There are lots of times on the bike, you’re out there 6am, freezing cold, dodging wallabies down in Tassie, and it’s not glamorous, but I think that’s what builds champions. And we’ve got two Tasmanians right here winning a gold medal. It speaks for itself.”



The Australian team’s victory continues its unbeaten run in the event at the Commonwealth Games. Since the team pursuit was introduced at the 2018 Games on the Gold Coast, Australia’s women have never lost. The women’s pursuit was one of three gold medals Australia won at the Chris Hoy velodrome on day one of the cycling in Glasgow, along with Tara Neyland, who set a new world record on her way to gold in the women’s C4-C5 individual pursuit, and the men’s sprint team, who won without former teammate Matthew Richardson. Richardson represented Australia until 2024, when he defected to England following the Paris Olympics. The allegiance switch was a shock to the Australian cycling team, including Leigh Hoffman, who earlier this week said Richardson “went on a holiday and never came back”. But the Australian team of Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Daniel James Barber managed to win without him – defeating England in the gold medal race. They didn’t, however, get the chance to race him. Richardson withdrew from the Games earlier this week after injuring himself in a crash during a world series race in Japan.



However, team officials told reporters Richardson wouldn’t have taken part in the team race anyway because he wouldn’t have arrived in Glasgow in time. Nevertheless, the Australian team said it was nice to get a win over England. Ryan Elliott, Daniel James Barber and Leigh Hoffman celebrate after winning gold. Getty Images Asked whether it was good to win without Richardson on the team, Hoffman said: “It would have been great if he stayed with Australia, but his heart was obviously never always in it. So, good riddance.” Among Australia’s other cycling medallists were Jessica Gallagher and pilot Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr, who won silver in the women’s tandem B sprint finals after a crash in the second of their three finals races.



Tandem riding is a para cycling event where a visually impaired athlete has a pilot at the front of the bike. The duo had a tyre failure, which caused the crash and forced them to rest before the Kiwis went on to win the final two races and clinch gold. Australia and New Zealand collide in the second of three races for the women’s tandem B sprint gold medal. Getty Images “When that tyre pressure literally disappears, you’re riding on carbon rims,” Mengler-Mohr explained. “It’s like going from being on roller skates to ice skates, and just sliding and having no traction. There’s nothing we could have done.”

World.title: George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage Ardee Napolitano July 31, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: Hollywood actor George Clooney and his British wife Amal, an international human rights lawyer, have evacuated their luxury home in south-eastern France as a result of the wildfires blazing in the region. The star behind the Ocean’s Eleven franchise and other films made the statement on Thursday (France time) in a letter to Didier Bremond, the mayor of the town of Brignoles, about 90 kilometres east of Marseille, Clooney’s publicist Guido Gotz said in an email. George and Amal Clooney. Alberto Pezzali/Invision/AP Addressed “Dear Didier”, the letter said the Clooneys had “no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment”. But as they evacuate Brignoles they wanted to assure Bremond that, whatever happened to the community, “we’ll be part of making it whole”, the letter said.



The Clooneys bought their home on a vineyard in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region in 2021 when it had an estimated value of about €9 million ($15 million). In an interview with Esquire last October, Clooney described their “farm in France” as their primary residence. The fire near Brignoles broke out Wednesday afternoon and burned some 100 hectares, local officials said. The blaze was far smaller than a vast inferno that has swept up the region around Bordeaux in southwestern France in recent days. The Clooneys’ vineyard estate in Brignoles. Backgrid About 700 residents from the areas near Brignoles had been evacuated, but were allowed to return to their homes on Thursday after the fire was brought under control, the officials said.



Water-bombing helicopters remained deployed over the area after the evacuation order was lifted, the regional administration said. It said weather conditions remained unfavorable, with high temperatures and winds expected to pick up again in the afternoon. Related Article Celebrity life Clooney takes swipe at Trump after dig over French citizenship The French government in December announced that the Clooneys along with their twins Ella and Alexander were awarded French citizenship. In the Esquire interview, Clooney said part of the impetus for the move to France was that he was “worried about raising our kids in LA, in the culture of Hollywood”. US President Donald Trump seemingly welcomed the news the pair had been granted French citizenship, calling them “two of the worst political prognosticators of all time” and claiming the actor was better known for his politics than his “totally mediocre movies”.



But George Clooney hit back, saying he also wanted to “make America great again” – starting with the US midterm elections in November. Related Article Updated

Bushfires ‘Doing their best to survive’: Inside Bordeaux’s wildfire refugee centre Europe is sweltering under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, creating tinderbox conditions for unprecedented fires that have flared from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean and forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate homes and vacation spots. Firefighters also battled flames in the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, Greece and Turkey on Thursday and were tamping down smouldering forests in southwest France where 224,000 people had been forced to flee. Romania shut down both reactors at its Cernavoda nuclear power plant due to low water levels in the Danube River used to cool them. In the Bordeaux region, wildfire evacuees streamed back to nine localities that authorities now deem safe after round-the-clock combat with the huge fire that ignited last week.



“It’s the first somewhat optimistic day,” said Sophie Brocas, prefect of Bordeaux’s Gironde region who gave the go-ahead for nearly two-thirds of the 224,000 evacuees to go home, including 60,000 allowed back to three Bordeaux suburbs on Tuesday. Authorities said the blaze is no longer growing beyond the 420 square kilometres already affected – an area four times that of Paris. A heat wave – France’s fourth of the year – gave way Thursday to cooler weather, higher humidity and even a little rain, helping the effort. A firefighting aircraft releases fire retardant in Lanton. “RiverCity Ferries won’t even match the Fair Work Commission’s own 4.75 per cent annual wage review increase or keep pace with inflation, claiming it is ‘not viable’ – all the while its parent company Kelsian Group’s own financial reports show substantial increases in revenue and profit,” the statement said. The signs have been posted at terminals around the city. Julius Dennis “The company’s CEO, executive leadership team and board have all received significant increases to their pay packages while our highly skilled and committed members that deliver the company’s service to the Brisbane public every day are being asked to accept an offer below inflation.” A RiverCity Ferries spokesperson said they were disappointed services would be disrupted. “We have been bargaining with the unions and employee representatives since October 2025 and remain committed to negotiating in good faith towards a fair and sustainable enterprise agreement,” they said.



“Our priority is to maintain safe and reliable ferry services wherever possible and minimise disruption to customers. We are working closely with Brisbane City Council and Translink to communicate any service impacts and to restore services as soon as possible.” A spokesperson for Transport and Main Roads said TMR is working with Brisbane City Council and RiverCity Ferries to minimise customer impacts. “This is a matter between RiverCity Ferries and their employees, and we encourage them to negotiate in good faith to reach an agreement as soon as possible.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe David Crowe Updated July 31, 2026 — 7:07am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of migrants have rushed across the border from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a startling move that was relayed on social media and triggered a political row about migration into Europe. One security official declared the border checkpoint had “totally collapsed” under pressure from the crowd, as young men spread instructions on social media on how to enter the Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa. Authorities said at least nine people had died trying to reach Ceuta from Morocco. Loading Some migrants swam from Moroccan territory to reach the Spanish enclave, while others walked around a breakwater and crossed the rocks in numbers that overwhelmed authorities. Spanish state television TVE reported that 2000 to 3000 people had crossed. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez promised an “immediate response” to the situation, as his critics blamed his migration laws for encouraging people to seek asylum in Spain and gain work rights in the European Union.



“We are mobilising all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible,” Sanchez said. Spain’s government later said it would send the military to help the Civil Guard “to maintain security in the city of Ceuta”. Thousands of people flood the border. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere The political impact reached far beyond Spain because of the debate across Europe about migration, with British right-wing leader Nigel Farage sharing the dramatic videos online.



“It’s time to wake up everybody,” Farage declared. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for urgent action and warned that her government might suspend an open-border passport agreement with Spain if the situation was not brought under control.



“The images coming from Ceuta are striking and demonstrate, once again, that uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe’s borders,” she said. “Italy will not stand by and watch. We are convening the relevant bodies, and following these meetings, we are prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain.” Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Civil Guard officers had to open the gates because they needed to prevent a bottleneck forming at the checkpoint.



Why are people fleeing Morocco? The rush follows a Supreme Court decision in Spain last month that protects migrants who are intercepted at sea while seeking to get to Ceuta, preventing them from being immediately returned to Morocco. That ruling is being blamed by some politicians for giving Moroccans an incentive to swim to Ceuta, a distance of about 2 kilometres across the water, or walk around the breakwater. There were chaotic scenes on the Ceuta shoreline. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Spanish police officers respond as migrants cross from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere



Another source of debate is the Sanchez government’s decision this year to grant an amnesty to migrants who were already in the country, leading to more than 1.3 million people applying to stay permanently. Ceuta, located roughly opposite Gibraltar in the western Mediterranean, has been a Spanish territory since 1580 and now has the status of an autonomous city of Spain, although it is surrounded by Moroccan territory. Spanish soldiers travel in military vehicles after being deployed to Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Rachid Sbihi, the head of the association that represents the Spanish Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, called for a national emergency to be declared in Madrid to stop the mass movement because the border had totally collapsed. “The situation is absolute chaos,” he said. “It’s not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing.”



The Ministry of the Interior in Madrid has pushed back at the idea of a national emergency being declared. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is due to travel to Ceuta on Friday. Migrants at the border of Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere The Mayor-President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the influx had overwhelmed the city’s ⁠reception system and left hundreds of migrants sleeping outside. “We are facing a situation ​of absolute humanitarian and social emergency,” Vivas told radio station Cadena SER, adding that facilities for ​unaccompanied minors were operating at 2400 per cent of capacity.



In comments to radio station Onda Cero, he described the situation as a national emergency and called for a “decisive, forceful, immediate and co-ordinated” response under a ​single command structure. Arrivals were currently averaging about 300 people a day, according to Vivas. At that pace, he warned, Ceuta could face a situation comparable to the May 2021 migration crisis, when 10,000 people entered ​the enclave in mere ​days. Belongings left behind by migrants float in the sea. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Vivas also pointed ⁠to the human cost of the crossings, saying 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months, and argued that ​stronger migration controls would help prevent further deaths. With AP, Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
The federal government is trying to stop a loophole in the NDIS that allows providers to claim for unproven therapies including wellness treatments and animal therapy.

Jenny McAllister, the federal minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme, has just been speaking on ABC Radio National.

She has told AM host Sally Sara that people had used the loophole to claim golf lessons.

“This is totally inappropriate. We’re cracking down on this through a number of means: changing the price guide, increasing our analytic capability, and seeking support from the parliament for new powers so we can continue to investigate providers who are doing the wrong thing.

“We made it very clear in 2024 that therapy needs to be delivered by a qualified practitioner, and that wellness supports or alternative therapies are not suitable.”

The loophole has existed since 2019 – but McAllister said when Labor had come into government, they were told the body administering the NDIA had “essentially no compliance mechanisms built into the NDIA by the Liberals”.

World.title: ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple reports iPhone sales surge Stan Choe Updated July 31, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A monster day for Microsoft’s stock following signals that its big spending on AI is translating into profits led a powerful rebound on Wall Street, while computer-chip companies regained some of their sharp recent losses. In the bond market, though, worries remained about inflation potentially remaining high for years. The S&P 500 rallied 1.7 per cent and more than recovered its drop from the day before, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 613 points, or 1.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, rallied 2.8 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a gain of 110 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. On Wall Street, Microsoft led the way and leaped 15.5 per cent for its best day in nearly 18 years after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Apple released its results after the closing bell, with sales and profits beating Wall Street expectations, fuelled by its customers snapping up iPhones and MacBooks amid price increases across the consumer electronics sector. Driving Apple’s results was a 21.7 per cent increase in iPhone sales to $US54.25 billion ($77.2 billion), above analyst estimates of $US53.86 billion, according to LSEG data. Those iPhone sales were Apple’s best-ever for a third quarter, when phone sales typically begin to slow as customers anticipate new models during the fall. Apple shares are 3.3 per cent lower in after-hours trade. Meta Platforms fell 8 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year.



Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying to power their AI efforts rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. Micron Technology jumped 18.4 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5 per cent. It was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft. Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 18 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13 per cent. On the losing end of Wall Street was Jersey Mike’s Subs. The sandwich chain’s stock fell 6 per cent in its first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. All told, the S&P 500 rose 121.48 to 7,437.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 613.92 to 52,208.06, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 679.24 to 25,122.18.



In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 4.67 per cent, the same as late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield ticked up to 5.22 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. Those yields move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite inflation remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.



“If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate. Reports released Thursday suggested the U.S. economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May’s level. In the oil market, prices eased. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to settle at $US86.88 per barrel.



It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. Seoul’s market has been at the centre of AI’s huge swings because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.title: Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Billie Eder July 31, 2026 — 6:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scroll down for a complete Commonwealth Games medal tally Glasgow: Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was flicking through her local newspaper in Tasmania in 2021 when she saw an  for a cycling talent search. Bored at home during the COVID-19 pandemic, she thought, why not show up and give it a crack? Five years on, Wilson-Haffenden is a Commonwealth Games champion after motoring home to win gold in the women’s team pursuit alongside Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks and Alyssa Polites after only starting the sport in 2021. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images



“I don’t think I can say this too loudly because COVID probably wasn’t great for a lot of people. But for me, it changed my life,” Wilson-Haffenden said. “I can’t be grateful for COVID, but I can be grateful for the outcome, that’s for sure.” Wilson-Haffenden, who was a hockey player at the time, was lucky to make it at all – she had to call in a favour and delay her tryout. “I actually couldn’t make it on the talent ID date, and called saying ‘I really want to give this a crack’,” she said. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images



“So they made a little allowance for me, but I just think it’s a message to all young kids, if you’re interested, give it a crack because you never know where it’ll take you.” She now spends most of the year in Girona – a cycling town in Catalonia, in the north-east of Spain – but said it was her formative cycling years in Tasmania that turned her into a champion. “I actually think it’s the cold mornings in Tassie that really build character – I think G [teammate Georgia Baker] will attest to it as well,” Wilson-Haffenden said. Tara Neyland broke a world record on her way to winning gold. Getty Images “It’s a pretty lonely sport. There are lots of times on the bike, you’re out there 6am, freezing cold, dodging wallabies down in Tassie, and it’s not glamorous, but I think that’s what builds champions. And we’ve got two Tasmanians right here winning a gold medal. It speaks for itself.”



The Australian team’s victory continues its unbeaten run in the event at the Commonwealth Games. Since the team pursuit was introduced at the 2018 Games on the Gold Coast, Australia’s women have never lost. The women’s pursuit was one of three gold medals Australia won at the Chris Hoy velodrome on day one of the cycling in Glasgow, along with Tara Neyland, who set a new world record on her way to gold in the women’s C4-C5 individual pursuit, and the men’s sprint team, who won without former teammate Matthew Richardson. Richardson represented Australia until 2024, when he defected to England following the Paris Olympics. The allegiance switch was a shock to the Australian cycling team, including Leigh Hoffman, who earlier this week said Richardson “went on a holiday and never came back”. But the Australian team of Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Daniel James Barber managed to win without him – defeating England in the gold medal race. They didn’t, however, get the chance to race him. Richardson withdrew from the Games earlier this week after injuring himself in a crash during a world series race in Japan.



However, team officials told reporters Richardson wouldn’t have taken part in the team race anyway because he wouldn’t have arrived in Glasgow in time. Nevertheless, the Australian team said it was nice to get a win over England. Ryan Elliott, Daniel James Barber and Leigh Hoffman celebrate after winning gold. Getty Images Asked whether it was good to win without Richardson on the team, Hoffman said: “It would have been great if he stayed with Australia, but his heart was obviously never always in it. So, good riddance.” Among Australia’s other cycling medallists were Jessica Gallagher and pilot Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr, who won silver in the women’s tandem B sprint finals after a crash in the second of their three finals races.



Tandem riding is a para cycling event where a visually impaired athlete has a pilot at the front of the bike. The duo had a tyre failure, which caused the crash and forced them to rest before the Kiwis went on to win the final two races and clinch gold. Australia and New Zealand collide in the second of three races for the women’s tandem B sprint gold medal. Getty Images “When that tyre pressure literally disappears, you’re riding on carbon rims,” Mengler-Mohr explained. “It’s like going from being on roller skates to ice skates, and just sliding and having no traction. There’s nothing we could have done.”

World.title: George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage Ardee Napolitano July 31, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: Hollywood actor George Clooney and his British wife Amal, an international human rights lawyer, have evacuated their luxury home in south-eastern France as a result of the wildfires blazing in the region. The star behind the Ocean’s Eleven franchise and other films made the statement on Thursday (France time) in a letter to Didier Bremond, the mayor of the town of Brignoles, about 90 kilometres east of Marseille, Clooney’s publicist Guido Gotz said in an email. George and Amal Clooney. Alberto Pezzali/Invision/AP Addressed “Dear Didier”, the letter said the Clooneys had “no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment”. But as they evacuate Brignoles they wanted to assure Bremond that, whatever happened to the community, “we’ll be part of making it whole”, the letter said.



The Clooneys bought their home on a vineyard in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region in 2021 when it had an estimated value of about €9 million ($15 million). In an interview with Esquire last October, Clooney described their “farm in France” as their primary residence. The fire near Brignoles broke out Wednesday afternoon and burned some 100 hectares, local officials said. The blaze was far smaller than a vast inferno that has swept up the region around Bordeaux in southwestern France in recent days. The Clooneys’ vineyard estate in Brignoles. Backgrid About 700 residents from the areas near Brignoles had been evacuated, but were allowed to return to their homes on Thursday after the fire was brought under control, the officials said.



Water-bombing helicopters remained deployed over the area after the evacuation order was lifted, the regional administration said. It said weather conditions remained unfavorable, with high temperatures and winds expected to pick up again in the afternoon. Related Article Celebrity life Clooney takes swipe at Trump after dig over French citizenship The French government in December announced that the Clooneys along with their twins Ella and Alexander were awarded French citizenship. In the Esquire interview, Clooney said part of the impetus for the move to France was that he was “worried about raising our kids in LA, in the culture of Hollywood”. US President Donald Trump seemingly welcomed the news the pair had been granted French citizenship, calling them “two of the worst political prognosticators of all time” and claiming the actor was better known for his politics than his “totally mediocre movies”.



But George Clooney hit back, saying he also wanted to “make America great again” – starting with the US midterm elections in November. Related Article Updated

Bushfires ‘Doing their best to survive’: Inside Bordeaux’s wildfire refugee centre Europe is sweltering under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, creating tinderbox conditions for unprecedented fires that have flared from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean and forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate homes and vacation spots. Firefighters also battled flames in the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, Greece and Turkey on Thursday and were tamping down smouldering forests in southwest France where 224,000 people had been forced to flee. Romania shut down both reactors at its Cernavoda nuclear power plant due to low water levels in the Danube River used to cool them. In the Bordeaux region, wildfire evacuees streamed back to nine localities that authorities now deem safe after round-the-clock combat with the huge fire that ignited last week.



“It’s the first somewhat optimistic day,” said Sophie Brocas, prefect of Bordeaux’s Gironde region who gave the go-ahead for nearly two-thirds of the 224,000 evacuees to go home, including 60,000 allowed back to three Bordeaux suburbs on Tuesday. Authorities said the blaze is no longer growing beyond the 420 square kilometres already affected – an area four times that of Paris. A heat wave – France’s fourth of the year – gave way Thursday to cooler weather, higher humidity and even a little rain, helping the effort. A firefighting aircraft releases fire retardant in Lanton. World.title: As it happened: Kiwi gold for David Liti, Emma Foy at Glasgow Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Leonard Powell live from Commonwealth Games Morning Report Download MP3 1m 43s

Another successful day for New Zealand at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, with gold medals to weightlifter David Liti and para-cyclist Emma Foy.

Both had to overcome the odds for victory, with Liti trailling his Indian rival by 10kg after the snatch and need a personal best 223kg clean and jerk to overcome the deficit. He had two attempts available, but he needed only one.

Foy and pilot Jessie Hodges fell behind Australia in the best-of-three sprint format at the velodrome, and were then involved in a crash with their rivals at the start of the second race.

After medical checks and track inspection, the Kiwis won the re-race and then commanded the deciding race for gold.

Shot putter Tom Walsh narrowly missed his attempt at a shot put hattrick, after winning at Gold Coast 2018 and Birmingham 2022, pipped in the penultimate round by Nigerian Chukwuebuka Enekwechi.

The women's team pursuit took silver behind Australia, while para-cyclist Nicole Murray and the men's pursuiters and para sprinter Anna Grimaldi all took bronze.

Murray briefly held the world record for the newly introduced 4000m individual pursuit for her C5 classification, but lost it within minutes to an Australian rival.

Another big day of medal prospects in store tonight, with our women's pole vaulters in action and more track cycling.

World.title: Samoa face World Rugby ban over prime minister's 'political madness', opposition warns
World.content:
Samoa's opposition leader Tuilaepa Sa'ilele Malielegaoi says the country faces suspension by World Rugby today because of "a dirty political move" by the government.

Tuilaepa's spoke to RNZ Pacific after the government announced that it was pulling its support of Lakapi Samoa due to "unresolved internal issues and division" at the national rugby union.

"The government does not provide the Samoa Rugby Union with any financial assistance, there are no internal issues, it's political madness on the part of the prime minister, " Tuilaepa, who is a former Samoan PM and the leader of the Human Rights Protection Party (HRPP), said.

RNZ Pacific understands World Rugby has given the Samoan government until Friday to accept a review of its decision to withdraw recognition and financial support of the rugby union.

Failure to accept the review or respond by the deadline could result in Samoa being suspended from international rugby for four years, according to Samoa Observer.

It added that the development follows a meeting between the Lakapi Samoa and World Rugby representatives on Thursday.

RNZ Pacific has contacted World Rugby, Lakapi Samoa and the Samoan government's press secretariat for a response to Tuilaepa's comments.

A World Rugby spokesperson said: "We are in active and constructive dialogue with all parties and remain focused on a positive resolution."

In February, Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt said the sport had been "politicised" and the status of the game in Samoa was poor. Manu Samoa

'World Rugby should not bend'

Tuilaepa, who stepped down as chairman of Lakapi Samoa in March, told RNZ Pacific he was not interested in whether the country faced suspension from international rugby.

"I was chairman (of Lakapi Samoa). I've done all that is possible for the good of rugby. If the new government comes in and doesn't support it, that's it," the former long-time prime minister said.

"I am not worried (about Samoa being suspended), if World Rugby wants to do that, that is the proper thing to do. Our people chose the government and therefore if our people suffer, that is what our country wants.

"World Rugby should not bend to a country where its leadership is so stupid it becomes involved in political decisions that are hurtful to the young people of our country," he said.

Tuilaepa added: "If the majority of Samoans end up regretting that young rugby players are banned at a world level, they should go and talk to the prime minister they voted for."

In February, Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa (La'auli) Leuatea Schmidt said the sport had been "politicised" and the status of the game in Samoa was poor.

"At this stage, our rugby is very impoverished ... we are at a level that Samoa has never been before, because of what? Because of management," Laauli said.

"We're coming in to clear out all the politicians inside our rugby union," he said at the time.

Tuilaepa stepped down as chairman of the Samoa Rugby Union a month later after his political stand-off with La'auli threatened to stall a new funding programme for the Pacific's three top rugby unions.

Laauli had refused to sign any new agreement with the Fijian and Tongan rugby unions until Tuilaepa and his board resigned and made way for new appointments.

The prime minister added that his government would set up a rival union to govern the sport in the country, if the entire Lakapi Samoa board did not resign.

World.title: Human Rights Watch report says Indonesia is silencing environmental activists in Papua
World.content:
A new Human Rights Watch (HWR) report says that the Indonesian government is silencing environmental activists in Papua region, known internationally as West Papua.

The report, titled Grabbed Land, Silenced Justice, examines how parts of Papua, in particular South Papua, are seeing a greater military presence in service of massive national development projects.

Indonesian govt silencing Papuan activists - report Pacific Waves Download MP3 3m

These projects, its argues, are causing mass deforestation and displacement throughout the province, directly threatening local livelihoods. All the while, journalists and activists who speak out tend to be arrested and mistreated.

HRW's Andrea Harsono, a lawyer and one of the report authors, told RNZ Pacific it is business as usual.

"More than a dozen laws in Indonesia are used to silence protests over environmental harms", he said.

"Authorities used provisions of the Plantation Law, the Mineral and Mining Law, the Job Creation Law, or the Prevention of Forest Destruction Law to prosecute all these indigenous leaders and environmentalists."

Harsono noted that while higher courts would typically throw these cases out, activists would be mistreated during their arrests and tied up fighting their case for months.

"Individual can spend months, even years, appearing before various law enforcement agencies to contest groundless claims against them."

It comes as forest fires continue to ravage South Papua, which activists say are exacerbated by the dead wood and dry land left by deforestation across million of hectares.

Google Maps

Every bulldozer has a soldier

South Papua has increasingly become the target of major Indonesian agricultural projects, most notably the Merauke Food and Energy Estate project, slated to cover roughly three million hectares.

The project would convert forests, wetlands, and savannas into rice fields, and sugarcane and palm oil plantations.

Harsono said that his sources on the ground in South Papua were reporting that land clearing had become increasingly militarised.

"Every bulldozer is accompanied by soldiers with semi-automatic weapons ... this is the only province of the six (Papuan provinces) that exists without armed (West Papuan pro-independence) movement against them," he said.

"It is easier to clear the swamps and the forests in South Papua compared with the other five provinces, where resistance is higher."

All the while, severe fire warnings are in place province-wide. According to spatial analysis from Indonesian NGO WALHI, most fire hotspots are concentrated in areas designated for the Food Estate program, and other projects such as palm oil.

The report also posited that the Indonesian government tends to under-report forest clearing, and by extension, Papua's vulnerability.

"West Papua has thick peatland, meaning that underneath the surface, if there is fire, the fire will keep on burning," Harsono explained.

"There are studies after studies showing unnatural death because of respiratory problems in Sumatra and Lakimantan, there is still no study about that in West Papua."

But Harsono said there was evidence of the impact of the large-scale environmental destruction in declining animal populations, loss of biodiversity, and downstream from that, community livelihoods.

"They used to hunt for deer, for cuscus who eat Saku trees - Saku trees are missing, sweet potatoes are missing."

Ambrosius Mulait, Bentala Pusaka Foundation

Food estate protesters targeted

The report claims that protesters of the food estate project are being actively targeted and silenced.

It points to an incident in January where police detained 11 Papuans who had protested about "risks to the customary land rights and livelihood of over 40,000 people" from the Indigenous Malind Anim people, including the groups Malind Makleuw, Malind Khimaima, and Yeinan.

It also reported a resident in the Ngguti District saying that the military compelled his family to leave their home for protesting, while the fear of appearing against the state drove them out of their village entirely.

Recently, RNZ Pacific reported the disappearance of Yasinta Moiwend, a Merauke resident who participated in the documentary Pesta Babi (or Pig Feast) that criticised the Merauke Food and Energy Estate project.

She had also filed two lawsuits against the government over its actions in relation to the project.

However, soon after the film's release, Moiwend's family said she was taken suddenly to Jakarta, where HRW reports they continue to believe she had been abducted, with an attempt to coerce her silence.

Moiwend is also reported to have subsequently criticised the film.

Harsono said that authorities attempt to silence activists, through intimidation, all the way up to physical abuse.

"If you are outspoken, if you are prominent, your family members or your children are put under pressure, or your livelihood, your job is disrupted, if not you losing your job."

Nevertheless, Harsono said he has seen no indication that activism within Papua will die down, especially among younger residents, who have no memory of life without Indonesian rule.

"If you take a look at the number of soldiers stationed in all the six provinces in West Papua, you will know that statistically, the ratio of a soldier to the population is getting lower," he said.

World.title: Winston Peters ‘inviting a sacking’ with attack on Chinese-born MP, Helen Clark says
World.content:
Helen Clark discusses Peters’ comments to Lawrence Xu-Nan Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Former Prime Minister Helen Clark says Winston Peters' comments about a Chinese-born Green MP appears to be "inviting a sacking".

On Wednesday, Peters told Lawrence Xu-Nan to "go back to your own country" during a debate in Parliament.

"That's where they lie like a flatfish, but they don't lie like that here, all right?" Peters said.

China has expressed its concerns about the remarks, which have been reported by the South China Morning Post.

Clark on Friday told Morning Report they were "very concerning" on two levels.

"Obviously on the level of an MP who came to New Zealand as a child, who's been here for 32 years ... I mean, this is quite extraordinary and I think sends a chill right around our migrant communities as to whether people are ever actually going to feel part of, and be welcomed in, New Zealand," she said.

"But then to add to that, you have the line around 'go back to your own country, where they lie like flatfish'. Now that country, of course, is a very great power, it's our largest trading partner - that is no way to speak about it.

"And you're left with this big concern of, can the foreign minister now manage the relationship with that key strategic partner? And the answer has to be, not really."

Clark believed a lot of different considerations would be going through Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's mind.

"Firstly, it seems to me that the behaviour of New Zealand First and of their leader, and of Shane Jones, has for some time been inviting a sacking, inviting a breakup of the coalition, and frankly, so close to an election campaign, that's probably, you know, neither here nor there.

"But there's also a point of view which says he's not only inviting sacking, he's inviting attention, so don't give it to him. But actually, in the end if you say nothing you seem complicit.

"When you're speaking in parliament you may think you have a hat on as New Zealand First leader but actually offshore you are going to be seen as the foreign minister and the statements that you make will either give credit to your country or they won't, and we know what the case is here.

"It's extremely difficult but I think that it does invite a sacking and the consequences that flow from that. In the end, you know, others have to be seen to stand for something and not for nothing, and to let this go I think is many steps too far."

Peters has been approached for comment.

In a social media post, Peters earlier said the outrage over his comments proved his point.

World.title: Magnitude 5.9 earthquake strikes Kermadec Islands region
World.content:
Earth Sciences New Zealand says a 5.9 magnitude earthquake has struck the Kermadec Islands region.

The islands are approximately 800-1000 kilometres northeast of the North Island.

The quake was recorded shortly before 10.30am on Thursday, about 200km away from Raoul Island, Geohazards duty officer Sheng-Lin Lin said.

There were no reports of damage and checks of GeoNet instruments have found all systems functioning as usual, Lin-Lin said.

There was no observed tsunami signal or unusual water levels.

Lin added that while the quake did not have a big impact it was a reminder that significant earthquakes can occur in this region and around Aotearoa.

No Earth Sciences staff were on the island at the time and it's not aware of anyone else being on the island. DOC also said it had no staff or contractors visiting the islands and no records of any other agencies, researchers or visitors being there.

World.title: Glasgow Commonwealth Games: Gold and records for Fiji's weightlifter Rainibogi
World.content:
Fiji's Taniela Rainibogi has a gold medal in the men's 110 kilogram weightlifting at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

He lifted 170kg in the snatch and 208kg in the clean and jerk - both Commonwealth Games records - for a total lift of 378kg, another Games record.

England's Cyrille Tchatchet II came second, lifting a total of 374 kg, and Canada's Xavier Lusignan got bronze, lifting 356kg.

Tonga's Joshua Uikilifi Jr came fourth, 25kg away from a medal.

Vanuatu's Thomas Wilbur and Samoa's Jack Opeloge did not finish.

Weightlifting Fiji head coach Henry Elder told FBC it hadn't been an easy road.

"We have been through this journey - there's been so many obstacles, so many challenges, so many ups and downs, and God has been faithful up until this very day. And it is to him and him alone that we give glory."

It's the Pacific's second gold and sixth medal in the Glasgow weightlifting program.

Also in weightlifting, David Liti took gold for New Zealand in the men's +110kg. Liti, while competing under the silver fern, is of Tongan heritage.

Meanwhile, Pacific athletes have been in action in the track and field overnight.

Cook Islands' Max Teuruaa is competing in the men's decathlon - a combination of 10 events - which continues into Saturday morning.

He threw a personal best in the decathlon shot put of 11.31 metres, which was 11th of 12 throws.

PNG's Scholastica Herman ran in the women's mile, and compatriot Adrine Monagi in the women's 100m hurdles, but they did not progress further.

In the men's javelin, PNG's Lakona Gerega finished 15th, and Tuvalu's Usufono Eneli 17th of 17 finishers, not qualifying for the final.

In the men's shot put, Nauru's Jonathan-Deiwea Detageouwa finished 10th with a season's best throw of 16.99 metres. Tonga's Penisimani Taeiloa finished with a 'no mark' result, meaning no valid trial was recorded.

World.title: Squishy dumpling toy banned overseas can still be ordered in New Zealand
World.content:
Consumer NZ is warning that gaps in Aotearoa's product safety system are leaving shoppers exposed, after finding a toy banned in the UK can still be bought here through online marketplaces.

A number of Squeezy Dumplings - a popular toy shaped like a soft dumpling - were recalled in the UK in June after testing found benzene in the outer layer.

Benzene can irritate the skin and, where exposure is significant, cause a burning feeling throughout the digestive tract.

While Consumer NZ said this recalled toy cannot be bought in stores like The Warehouse or Kmart, it can be ordered from Aliexpress.

Stores such as The Warehouse and Kmart do, however, sell similar products.

Head of research and advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said the availability of potentially dangerous toys through online marketplaces exposed a weakness in how product safety is managed in New Zealand.

"Shoppers shouldn't have to wonder whether a toy is safe. Yet for many products sold online, there has been no independent testing before they reach New Zealand homes."

She said New Zealand product safety laws had not been significantly updated in decades, while in-store and online marketplaces had changed dramatically.

New Zealand has a product safety standard for children's toys enforced by the Commerce Commission.

However, Rasmussen said the system was far from watertight and there remained a risk that unsafe products cross into the country every day.

"That system only works if manufacturers are doing the right thing and problems are identified quickly," Rasmussen said.

"Unfortunately, that's not always the case."

Earlier this month, research by Auckland University of Technology confirmed asbestos was present in some children's play sand sold in New Zealand and that airborne fibres could be released during normal play.

Rasmussen said the safety regime currently used by New Zealand and Australian regulators was heavily reliant on risk assessments commissioned by product suppliers themselves, rather than independently verified testing.

"Whether it's asbestos in play sand or benzene in a toy, these cases demonstrate why we cannot rely solely on manufacturers' own safety claims."

World.title: Is Australia losing its shine?
World.content:
What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

A promise of a better life in Australia has drawn many New Zealanders across the Tasman in recent years. But economists say the tide may be about to turn.

As the economy slowed after the post-Covid boom, the number of New Zealanders migrating to Australia picked up. There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, smaller than the 31,100 in 2024 but much higher than the 3000 a year that was normal between 2014 and 2019.

The record was a loss of 43,700 in the year to March 2012.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people were drawn to Australia because the country was richer and had become steadily more so than New Zealand for the last 40 years.

Australia's GDP per person started to diverge from New Zealand's in the 1970s and is now significantly higher.

Eaqub said that was partly because of their commodity prices and a better terms of trade but it was not only mining that helped. New Zealanders were earning less on average and spending more of their income on housing.

But he said where New Zealand's house price relative to GDP per person, and rents relative to GDP had been higher for a long time, they were starting to converge.

"For a long time, New Zealand's housing market has just been really terrible in terms of how unaffordable it is, both in terms of house prices and rents… we spend a lot more of our income on housing compared to Australia, everything else is much the same.

Susan Edmunds on the Australia migration trend Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"Ours has got a little bit better and theirs has got a lot worse."

Eaqub said the current slowdown in Australia's housing market could change the picture again but New Zealand had made more progress with its conversation about public policy and housing in recent years than Australia had.

"I'm not saying we're perfect but I think it's far more mature here than it is over there."

He said Australia's economy also had headwinds and unemployment rising, which might discourage people from moving there if their access to welfare was likely to be limited. Australia also has higher central bank interest rates with similar levels of inflation.

A comparison of house prices relative to GDP per capita in Australia and New Zealand from 1995 until 2025. Supplied / Simplicity

There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, Supplied / Qantas

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones agreed there were signs that "some of those economic relativities are starting to tilt more towards New Zealand".

"Probably more so from the Australian side as the Aussie economy slows down. Household spending growth there is entering a softer patch alongside falling house prices and a likely further rise in unemployment. As an example, New Zealand job ads have been, tentatively, rising against a flat-to-lower trend in Australia. That's historically quite a good indicator to suggest some narrowing in the big gap between New Zealand and Aussie unemployment rates is likely. That subtle shift in labour market relativities is I think one of the key reasons why New Zealand departures to Australia have slowed up a little."

He said he would still frame it more as New Zealand catching up rather than overtaking.

"Australia's economy starts from an outright stronger position in nearly all areas. Our forecasts do have New Zealand growth catching up and eventually overtaking that of Australia over the next 12-18 months, but it could be quite a while before New Zealand's unemployment rate falls down to where Australia's resides in the mid-to-late 4s."

ANZ senior economist Miles Workman said the two economies had been on different paths for a while.and New Zealand had more of a "boom-bust" Covid experience than Australia.

"That's likely to remain the case for a while yet, with New Zealand starting from a weaker position than Australia in terms of economic momentum, meaning the hurdle to growth in New Zealand should be a bit lower. The starting point for the respective housing markets is a similar story.

"The difference in unemployment rates between Australia and New Zealand helps explain the trans-Tasman migration cycle. Our forecasts have that gap narrowing from late this year, which should reduce some of the incentive to move purely for cyclical labour market reasons.

"However, it will take more than a few years of business cycle divergence to address the more structural income differential between the two countries. Even if New Zealand's economy outperforms Australia's for a period, skilled workers will likely still be able to earn materially more in Australia doing similar work. Australia's labour market is also larger, with more major cities, industries and career opportunities to choose from."

He said it was possible New Zealand would start to look more attractive over the next little while, because it was coming off a weaker base.

"Closing the gap with Australia in a more structural sense would require stronger productivity growth over the long run, which is what ultimately drives higher incomes. A cyclical upswing alone is unlikely to be enough."

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod last year argued that New Zealand's economic growth was likely to outpace Australia's.

World.title: Australia's old friend wasn't at the Glasgow velodrome, but the old enemy was
World.content:
The crowds at the 2026 Commonwealth Games have varied in size and spirit.

Particularly at the Scottish Event Campus, not far from the city centre, casual fans will wander down and get a taste of the action if they've got time on their weekend.

It's school holiday time in Glasgow too, so plenty of families looking for a way to occupy the kids have made their way into the various arenas.

You may never get the chance to watch again, so a spot of 3x3 basketball or bowls, accompanied by some frankly excellent tunes and an overpriced carton of chips, is a decent way to spend four hours.

Aussie sprint stars through to 200m finals, gold rush at the velodrome Australia's track cycling squad claims three golds on the first day of competition at the velodrome, as Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis fly into their second finals of the week.

That's especially true when the weather has been so dreary to start the Games.

But on a day when it dried out at last, thousands made a decidedly purposeful pilgrimage to the velodrome at the Glasgow International Arena, just next to the home ground of Celtic Football Club.

This was not something you happen upon. This was something you go to. This was the moment Scotland had been waiting for at the arena named for one of their favourite sons, Sir Chris Hoy.

Ironically, before every race it was a pre-recorded Sir Chris (the real thing might have caused a riot) and fellow Scottish icon Duncan Scott telling the crowd to quiet down — or "haud yer wheesht", as Scott said — for the starter's buzzer.

But even Hoy — the six-time Olympic, 11-time world and two-time Commonwealth cycling champion — couldn't have contained his house when it was Scotland's Neil Fache (along with pilot Aaron Pope) who won the first gold of the track cycling program for these Games in the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

Scots Neil Fachie MBE (left) and pilot Aaron Pope won the first gold medal of the cycling program in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Australian Kane Perris won Australia's first medal in that event alongside pilot Luke Zaccaria, and earlier in the day, Tara Neyland had picked up Australia's first world record in any event at these Games when she clocked 4:49.648 in qualifying for the C4-5 4,000m individual pursuit.

She later went on to win gold, but only after the women's team pursuit squad started what the cycling team hopes will be a gold rush in Glasgow.

Trailing New Zealand at the halfway mark of the gold medal race against New Zealand, the team of Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden put away their schedule and just started racing.

"That's my happy place. When we start racing, that's when I'm happiest. When the board goes away, and the hand signals come out, that's when I come into my own," 21-year-old gun Wilson-Haffenden said.

Women's team pursuit gold marked the start of what promises to be a big Games for Australian cycling. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"Just pedal. I was riding 50-cent coins by the end, the pedals weren't going around smooth but giving as much power as I had, grit the teeth and get to the finish line."

England pipped their men's counterparts, and Jessica Gallagher was unable to defend her Birmingham gold in the tandem B sprint final after a tyre failure caused a nasty crash with the New Zealanders in the second race.

But, as pilot Jacqui Mengler-Mohr put it: "It's not how many times you fall, it's how many times you get back up."

Silver medallists Jessica Gallagher (right) and Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr (left) had a nasty fall as they won tandem B sprint silver. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

And getting back up was exactly what the men's team sprinters did, going one better than the women's team and taking down their English rivals in the final.

They never looked like getting caught over the 1,000m race as Leigh Hoffman won a title as the leader of a new-look team with 23-year-old Danny Barber and 22-year-old Ryan Elliott.

The revamp came after the defection of Olympic gold medallist and sprint superstar Matthew Richardson, whose name Elliott wouldn't even utter when talking about the rivalry with Team England.

"I think it's definitely grown a lot since the swap and defection," he said.

"Between the GB guys maybe a bit less so but definitely between the defector himself."

Australian defector Richardson out of Games after fall Matt Richardson, a three-time Olympic medallist in Paris for Australia before he sensationally defected to the land of his birth, has been ruled out of the Commonwealth Games.

He wasn't the only departure after the team's gold medal at the Paris Olympics, with Matthew Glaetzer retiring and Tom Cornish pivoting to endurance events, making way for Elliott and Barber.

"There's a big change in the roster after Paris, and everyone's question then is: how well can our system back up? What's their depth?" he said.

"Us as the younger guys coming through wanted to prove we have depth in Australia and we're here because we're hungry."

Hoffman said he enjoyed riding with teammates who were 100 per cent in it for Australia.

Ryan Elliott, Danny Barber and Leigh Hoffman won team sprint gold in their new formation. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"It would've been great if he stayed with Australia but his heart was obviously never always in it, so good riddance," he said.

Richardson is no longer coming to Glasgow at all due to an ugly fall during a keirin race in Japan just days ago, with Hoffman disappointed he and Barber won't get a crack at him in the individual event.

"I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how I and Danny stack up against him," Hoffman said.

"I'm upset he's not here, but that is what it is. … I've got plenty of other fish to worry about."

England, Wales, Scotland, Australia and New Zealand are some of the world's strongest track cycling nations, with Malaysia's Azizul Awang and Nicholas Paul from Trinidad and Tobago threats for Hoffman and Barber.

But the good news is Hoffman isn't going anywhere.

"We checked his passport and his lineage," Elliott said.

"So he's good."

World.title: Ex-MAFS star Ridge Barredo sticking to weightlifting despite ugly injury
World.content:
Ridge Barredo's description of the knee injury that ended his Commonwealth Games weightlifting campaign is enough to turn most of us off even watching the sport for good.

"I heard it pop on the third attempt, I tried to give it my all and I heard it pop [out] and pop back in," he said of his failed third snatch attempt in the men's 110kg class.

"Just to feel it was a little bit scary. Initial pain was an eight or nine out of 10."

Barredo said it was the first time he had ever experienced an injury like that, sustained as he tried to throw 162 kilograms over his head.

Loading Instagram content

By the time he spoke to media, having been helped off the Armadillo stage, he said he was just "a little bit uncomfortable" and described the pain as down to a six or seven out of 10.

This was his third Commonwealth Games and the 30-year-old vowed to be back at Amdavad in four years.

"It's not the end. I'm still relatively young, still hungry for it, still want to be the best in Australia," he said.

"I'm not done yet, no way. Not a chance. I'll be back for sure. Four times, watch, mark my words."

And he said this difficult and painful journey is still preferable to a return to the scene that made his descriptor on Google not "athlete" or "weightlifter", but "internet personality".

That's thanks to his turn on reality TV show Married At First Sight three years ago.

One of only a handful of successful couples from the program, Barredo and wife Jade are still together.

Loading Instagram content

Jade and daughter Victoria were in the crowd watching as he suffered his injury.

And while the program worked out for him, Barredo says his TV days are over.

"My TV career is definitely done, I've found my partner. I'm off reality TV. Wouldn't recommend it," he said.

"If you want to have some fun in a toxic environment, go for it, but personally I wouldn't be going back."

He's not the only Games athlete shunning the reality TV scene (for now) with Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan revealing she had to make a choice to continue swimming or go on Love Island last year.

'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance' An unexpected source kicks off another record-breaking night for Australian swimming as we get implicit and explicit reminders that we shouldn't take this for granted.

Shanahan opted not to enter the villa, ultimately winning silver in the women's 200m backstroke on the first night of the Glasgow swimming program.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season," Shanahan told BBC Scotland.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."
